activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2018 World Cup in Russia was the first to use video assistant referees, who can review goals, penalties, direct red cards and cases of mistaken identity.
story:
The projector screen hung between two goalposts on the community field, sagging in the middle like a hammock, and every adult in the picnic area had an opinion about whether that would ruin the picture. It didn't, quite, though the middle of the pitch in Moscow bent downward whenever the ball crossed it. Carson sat on a folding chair between his mother and Tyrese, a plate of his uncle's ribs going cold on his lap, and watched the World Cup match that Ms. Chen had organized the whole afternoon around. She taught chemistry at the high school and had, for reasons no one could pin down, underwritten the entire event: the projector, the extension cords, the rented screen, even the popcorn machine humming behind the bleachers like a small turbid river of melted butter.

"It's the first World Cup with this," Tyrese said during a lull in the second half, gesturing at the screen with a chicken wing. "VAR. Video assistant referees. They can review goals, penalties, direct red cards, and cases of mistaken identity."

"Mistaken identity," Carson's mother repeated, in the tone she used for things she suspected were inventions of the young.

"It's real," Tyrese said. "Russia 2018. The whole tournament. First time." He would not have known it himself except that Mattea had made him a study guide two months ago, back when they'd all pretended to care about the group stage for a class project on international broadcasting rights, a project that had mostly consisted of eating chips and arguing about camera angles.

Then the thing happened. A forward went down in the box in the eighty-fourth minute, the referee pointed to the spot, and the stadium noise changed pitch, and a little box appeared in the corner of the sagging screen. VAR CHECK: PENALTY. The whole picnic groaned as one organism. His uncle began a lecture on how the game had survived a hundred years without cameras and would now die of waiting, and Ms. Chen said something about throughput, about how reviews were supposed to speed up justice and instead had created a bottleneck, and nobody could agree on whether the wait was thirty seconds or four minutes because time behaves strangely when two dozen people are all staring at the same rectangle.

While the adults argued, Carson noticed a smaller crisis unfolding behind the bleachers. The kids' game, the one that had been running all afternoon on the far half of the field with a cone for a goal, had stopped. Mattea stood with the ball under her arm and a boy of about eleven in front of her, both of them furious in the specific way of people who know the game cannot continue until someone wins an argument.

"He was offside," Mattea said when Carson wandered over, arbiter-shaped merely by being seventeen. "He was past the last defender when the ball was played. I saw it."

"You didn't," the boy said. "You were running the other way. You couldn't have."

And there it was, Carson thought, the whole problem in miniature: a game that runs on what humans can see, and a truth that does not care what humans can see. On the screen behind them, the referee in Russia stood with a hand to his ear, waiting for a verdict from a room he would never enter, delivered by people the crowd could never question. Out here there was no room, no review, no tape. There was only Mattea's certainty and the boy's certainty, and eleven other kids getting bored enough to start eating dandelions.

"What would VAR do," Carson asked, mostly to himself, but Mattea heard him.

"They only review goals, penalties, direct red cards, and mistaken identity," she said, ticking them off like a grocery list. "Not offside. Not unless it leads to a goal. So even out there, no review. It'd just be the linesman's call."

"But there's no linesman."

"Exactly. There's you."

He stood there for a second, feeling the weight of it. Part of him wanted the camera, wanted the clean authority of a fact replayed from three angles. Another part remembered his uncle's groan, the dead air of the whole picnic hanging on a man with a finger to his ear, and wondered whether certainty bought that way cost something. Maybe the game was better when you accepted that seeing was limited and moved on anyway. Or maybe that was just a comfortable thing adults said when the truth had gone against them once too often. He honestly could not decide, and the not-deciding was itself a kind of information.

"Okay," Carson said. "Mattea, you called it as you saw it. That's your job out here, you're the closest thing to an official. But," and he held up a hand before the boy could protest, "since there's no review and I can't overrule without evidence, the call stands, and we take a two-minute water break, and next goal wins so nobody has time to file an appeal."

"That's not fair," the boy said.

"It's not," Carson agreed. "It's soccer."

The boy stared at him for a long moment, then laughed, one short bark of it, and jogged back toward the cone. Behind them, the picnic erupted: on the sagging screen, the referee had turned to the crowd and drawn a small rectangle in the air, and the penalty stood. The uncle threw his napkin into the air like a matador. Carson picked up the ball, bounced it once on the grass, and rolled it to Mattea.

"Play," she said, and pointed down the field.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: Melodies are often built from four-bar phrases, so a sixteen-bar melody commonly falls into four phrases.
story:
The assignment on the board said sixteen bars, chord changes included, notation by Friday, and Gavin had spent Tuesday evening filling a page with fragments that went nowhere. He sat in the back of the music room during lunch with his staff paper in front of him, pencil hovering over bar five, unable to make the tune go anywhere.

"It sounds like a ringtone," Lia said, leaning over from the next chair. She had finished hers on Monday, some flowing thing in G major that Ms. Fischer had already pinned above the piano.

"It doesn't sound like anything. It stops." He played the four bars he had, then the four bars after them, and the second group had nothing to do with the first. "I keep trying to write one long line and it dies in the middle."

Romy slid into the seat on his other side and put half a sandwich on the edge of his paper. "Play the beginning again." He did. "Okay, that's a sentence. Like you said something and now you have to say it three more times."

Gavin looked at his page. Four bars. He counted the empty staves below them, drew a light double bar after the fourth measure, then another after the eighth, the twelfth. Four boxes. He had been thinking of the melody as one long breath, and it kept collapsing, but if each box only had to hold one small thought, that seemed possible. The third box could answer the first. The last could slow down, land somewhere quiet.

"That's how you're splitting it?" Lia asked.

"Melodies are built from four-bar phrases," he said, mostly to himself, numbering the boxes. "So sixteen bars would be four of them."

Ms. Fischer crossed the room and stood behind them, saying nothing. Gavin's ears went hot, expecting to be told the boxes were wrong, that he was dodging the hard part. She tapped the third phrase with her finger.

"What's this one doing?"

"I don't know yet. Maybe the same as the first but higher. Or lower."

"Write both and choose later." She moved on toward the piano, where a freshman was mangling a C major scale, and Gavin turned back to his paper before she could change her mind about him.

He worked through Thursday, and it was slower than he wanted. The second phrase kept fighting him; he wrote a version that climbed, hated it, wrote one that fell back to the opening note, liked that better. He tried suturing the phrases together with a held note at each seam so the melody wouldn't sound chopped up, and it helped, though he wasn't sure it was a real technique or just something he'd invented. His dad, watching from the kitchen doorway while Gavin played it on the keyboard app, said it sounded like weather changing, which Gavin decided to take as a compliment since his dad usually compared everything to either traffic or meat.

Romy had become the room's pundit on all things theory, mostly because he'd watched forty minutes of videos about voice leading and now offered opinions to anyone with paper on their desk. On Thursday he informed Gavin that his chord in bar eleven was "objectively ugly." Gavin played it again, then played it resolving to the chord he'd put in bar twelve.

"It's supposed to be ugly there. Then it isn't."

"It's still ugly."

"That's the point of it being there." He wasn't sure that was true. It might genuinely be ugly, and he might be dressing up a mistake as a choice. He underlined the chord in pencil so he could come back to it.

By Friday morning he had sixteen bars he could play all the way through, and he'd written it out in ink, beams and stem directions checked twice against the notation handout. He got to the music room early, while the hallway outside was still crepuscular, the fluorescent lights not yet fully awake, and put his page on the piano. He played it at performance speed for the first time. The third phrase came in and it did sound like the first one, lifted, and the fourth slowed and landed, and the held notes held.

Lia appeared in the doorway with her bag on one shoulder. "Bar eleven still ugly?"

"Objectively." He played the chord, let it hang, and resolved it. "Play it with me. Top line, from the top."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: Google added 'search by image' in 2011, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web.
story:
The message from her mother arrived during sixth period: come to the office after school, there's something you should see. Violet took the bus downtown, signed in at the front desk with a pen tied to a clipboard, and rode the elevator to the eleventh floor, where her mother worked in a cubicle with a small cactus and a photograph of Violet at age nine, missing two teeth.

"Your grandmother sent me something," her mother said, spinning her chair around before Violet had even set down her backpack. On the screen was a forwarded email, all caps in the subject line, with a photo attached: a bridge buckled in the middle, cars dangling, a plume of black smoke. "It says this happened this morning on the interstate near us. She's asking if we're safe. She's asking if you're safe. I was about to forward it to the whole family."

Violet leaned over her mother's shoulder. The photo had that too-perfect quality, the smoke almost painted, and something in her stirred, the vague suspicion she'd been trying to discipline all semester. Fatoumata had a rule she repeated like a chant: nothing goes out of your phone until you know where it came in. Dominik had broken the rule once and spent a week apologizing for a fake evacuation notice that emptied half the cafeteria. Violet had watched both of them and arrived somewhere in the middle, unsure, not wanting to be either the fool or the smug one.

"Wait," she said. "Don't forward it yet."

"Why? Look at it. That's a bridge. That's smoke."

"That's the problem. I can't tell when it's from." Violet pulled the desk chair over, sat down, and dragged the photo onto her own phone with a cable from her mother's drawer. Then she opened a search engine, the one her civics teacher, Ms. Littlechild, had made them use for a project on rumor in elections. In the image search bar there was a small camera icon. "Watch this," Violet said, half to her mother and half to herself, because she had only done it twice before and one of those times it had failed.

She clicked the icon, chose the option to upload the picture, and attached the file. "Google added search by image in 2011," she said, mostly to steady herself. "You can upload a picture, or paste its link, and it finds where else it shows up on the web." The page thought for a moment, that particular suspenseful blankness, and then returned a stack of results.

The oldest hit was from nine years ago. The same buckled bridge, the same painted smoke, the same dangling cars, over a headline about an earthquake in a country neither of them had ever thought about at breakfast. There were later appearances too, a dozen of them, the photo re-dressed in new catastrophes like a costume, each one insisting on a fresh date and a fresh location. Near the bottom of the list was a fact-checking site with the image stamped in red.

"Huh," her mother said.

"Huh," Violet agreed. She screenshotted the results and started typing a reply to her grandmother, then deleted it, then typed again, then deleted it again. It was hard to find a tone that wasn't a lecture. Her grandmother had grown up in a world where a photograph in a newspaper was as good as sworn testimony, and there was something almost touching about that trust, and something almost dangerous too.

"I'll write it," she said finally, and composed it like a small essay, though she tried to make it read like a granddaughter.

"Hi Grandma. The bridge is real but the story isn't. I did a search where you upload the picture and it finds every other place it's appeared, and this one is nine years old, from an earthquake far away. Somebody gave it a new caption and it's been circulating ever since. I can show you how to do it yourself at Thanksgiving, it takes about a minute. Please don't forward it to Aunt Carol, she'll panic. Love, Violet."

She read it aloud. Her mother laughed, a real laugh that startled the man in the next cubicle, who put his head over the partition like a prairie dog and then withdrew. "Aunt Carol would absolutely panic," her mother said. "She'd put water in the bathtub."

Send. Then Violet sat for a moment with the cursor still blinking in the empty reply box. She felt the small clean satisfaction of a thing checked, and underneath it a wriggling discomfort she decided not to smooth over. She could verify this photo, but plenty of others she'd forwarded over the years she had never verified, and her culpability didn't disappear just because she'd caught one. The putative disaster had never existed, and yet her grandmother's fear had been real, and so, for one bus ride, had Violet's own quickened pulse. She didn't know yet where the line was between healthy skepticism and believing nothing, between her own caution and Fatoumata's certainty, and she suspected the line moved. That unsettled her more than the fake bridge had.

"You okay?" her mother asked.

"Yeah. Just thinking about how many things I've shared without looking." Violet pocketed her phone. "I want to actually get good at this. Not just lucky."

Her mother turned back to her spreadsheet and the cactus and the gap-toothed photograph. Violet stood, shouldered her backpack, and on her way to the elevator pulled up her chat with Fatoumata and typed, "Grandma sent a fake disaster photo. I caught it. Teach me the stuff you know." Then she pressed the down button and watched the numbers descend toward her.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L. (2021), the Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a school violated a student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post.
story:
The assignment on the board read "Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L." and beneath it, in Mr. Sok's cramped handwriting, "Argue both sides. You draw the school's position first." William copied it into his notebook without enthusiasm, because arguing the school's side of anything felt like defending a hallway monitor with a gavel.

He started that evening at his desk, case file open on his laptop, becoming for two hours a kind of autodidact of First Amendment law: opinions, summaries, a podcast where two law professors talked past each other. The basic facts came clear quickly. A student had posted something scathing about her cheerleading squad on Snapchat, off campus, on a weekend, and the school had suspended her from the team. The Supreme Court had taken the case in 2021. William wrote the citation on an index card and turned it over, saving the outcome for later, the way he saved the last bite of a meal.

Emmitt found him in the library the next morning, hunched over a legal pad covered in arrows. "You're doing the Snapchat one," Emmitt said, dropping into the chair across from William. "Ayaan has the locker search case. He's thrilled."

"I have to argue the school's side first," William said. "Then the student's. Same afternoon."

"That's insane. How do you believe both?"

William didn't answer, because he didn't know yet, and admitting that to Emmitt would make it permanent. Instead he drafted the school's argument: discipline, team cohesion, the coach's authority, the way an off-campus post could poison a locker room. The words came easily, which bothered him. They sounded like something a vice principal would say over a PA system.

The afternoon of the mock court, Room 214 had been rearranged into a semicircle, and Mr. Sok sat at the front table wearing, inexplicably, a tie with tiny scales of justice on it. Ayaan presided as chief judge, radiating the joy of someone finally allowed to say "overruled." William stood, laid out the school's case, and sat down. Then he flipped his index card over to prepare for round two, and it was only then, reading his own handwriting, that he saw what he had saved: the Court had ruled 8-1 that the school violated the student's free speech by punishing the post. Eight justices against one. The school's side, the side he had just argued with such fluency, had lost before he was born into the case.

Standing again, he felt the strange doubling of his position. He argued the student's side now, and every point he had made an hour earlier turned in his hands like a coin. The post was off campus. It was a weekend. The Court had said, eight to one, that punishing it violated her free speech. But in the middle of his rebuttal he stopped, because he was about to say that schools should never reach past their gates, and he did not entirely believe it. He had seen what a group chat could do to a kid by Monday morning. Everyone in that room had.

"I want to concede something," William said, and the room went quiet in the way rooms do when someone breaks the script. "The Court ruled 8-1 that the school violated her free speech. But they left room. Schools aren't powerless off campus. So the question isn't whether the school can punish the post. It's whether it should have, in this case, for this reason. And I think the answer is no, but I can't prove it's always no."

Ayaan looked at Mr. Sok, who made a small go-ahead gesture. "Ruling from the bench," Ayaan said, trying to sound bored and failing. "Judgment for the student. Counsel is reminded that the winning side was the one willing to lose a point."

Afterward, packing up, William found Emmitt waiting by the door. "Both sides," Emmitt said. "Which one do you actually believe?"

William slid the index card into his notebook, blank side up. "Ask me which one I believe on a day when I'm not the one who posted it."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: For US federal Direct Subsidized student loans, the government pays the interest while the student is in school; unsubsidized loans build interest during that time.
story:
Leah sat in the passenger seat of a Corolla she could not afford, watching her mother run a finger along the stitching of the steering wheel while a salesman leaned against the door frame and talked about low monthly payments. He had a voice like warm syrup. He kept saying the word "only," and every time he said it, the number attached to it got smaller, which Leah understood, even at seventeen, was the whole trick.

"Can we see the loan paper?" Leah asked. "The part with the interest rate."

Her mother glanced at her, that warning look, the one that said don't embarrass me. The salesman smiled without moving his eyes.

"Of course," he said, and produced a folder from somewhere as if it had always been in his hand.

They were at the dealership because their own car, the ten-year-old Civic, had died on the highway entrance ramp two weeks before, and Leah's mother worked the early shift at the hospital, and the bus did not run there before six in the morning. That was the want. That was the whole reason they were being handed complimentary bottled water in a room that smelled like new plastic and ambition.

Leah looked at the paper. She had spent the weekend with two other papers spread on her bed: her financial aid letter from the college she would start in the fall, with its two loan offers side by side. One was subsidized, one was not. She had read that line about the subsidized one maybe forty times, and the unsubsidized one maybe forty more, and slowly something had assembled itself in her head, like a photograph developing. The subsidized loan, the government paid the interest while she was in school. The unsubsidized loan, interest built during those years, quietly, while she was reading essays and forgetting about it. The same borrowed money could cost more or less depending on which kind it was, and the difference was time.

She thought about that now, in the dealership, watching the salesman's pen hover over the monthly payment figure. Seventy-two months. Six years. He had not said the total.

"What's the total?" she asked. "With the interest. What does the car actually cost by the end?"

The room went quiet in a way that felt engineered. Another customer, a man in a golf shirt, looked over. The salesman laughed, a small sound, and said something about how nobody thought like that anymore, how that was her grandfather's economics.

"My daughter's very smart," her mother said, and there was something complicated in it, pride folded over irritation.

At school, Cindy had called Leah a sycophant once, in the fall, for laughing at a joke a teacher made that wasn't funny, and Leah had thought about the word for weeks. She didn't want to be the person who made herself pleasant to power. But she also didn't want to be the person who performed intelligence at her mother's expense, in public, in front of a man whose job was to be smooth. There was a version of this where she stayed quiet. There was a version where she was grandiose about it, announced the whole lecture about compound interest like she was running a seminar. She had watched a boy in her econ class do exactly that in September, and nobody had liked him after, and it had stigmatized him for the rest of the term, honestly, that one performance of knowing.

So she said, evenly, "I just want to know the number. My student loans, I've been comparing them all weekend. One of them builds interest while I'm in school and one doesn't, so the same money costs different amounts. I figure a car works the same way."

The salesman looked at her mother instead of her. "Shall we give you two a minute?"

"Yes," her mother said.

The minute lasted longer than a minute. Leah found the total cost line on the contract herself, followed it with her finger, and her mother read it, and then read it again, and then set the paper down on the hood of the Corolla with great care, as though it might go off. The number was almost double the sticker price. Six years of "only" added up to that.

"There's a used lot on Miller Road," Leah said. "Ana's brother bought there. They show you the totals."

"I know," her mother said. She was quiet for a second, gathering her purse, and Leah could not tell if what she felt was anger at the salesman or something older and heavier that had nothing to do with him. "I wanted it to be simple. Just once."

They left the folder on the hood and walked out past the row of gleaming hoods, past the water bottles, past the golf shirt man who was now signing something. At the door, the salesman called out a lower number, and then a lower one, and Leah realized she would never know which of those, if any, had been the real one.

On the used lot on Miller Road, an older Civic sat in the third row, dull blue, honest. The dealer there, an older woman with reading glasses on a chain, slid the paper across and circled the final total before anyone asked. Her mother asked about a smaller down payment so the fall tuition deposit could survive, and Leah sat doing quiet arithmetic on her phone, the subsidized and unsubsidized amounts, the interest that would or would not accumulate over four years, the shifts her mother would need to cover the rest. She could not make all of it fit yet. Some of it she would figure out as she went, and some of it, she suspected, she would simply find out later, the way you find out most things.

Her mother came back from the office jingling a key. "You drive," she said, and tossed it across the lot.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: JUnit's assertEquals takes the expected value first and the actual value second, so swapping them gives confusing failure messages.
story:
The pit at the regional robotics competition smelled like solder and vending machine coffee, and James had spent the first forty minutes of practice matches doing nothing but staring at a laptop screen. His team's scouting app, the one he'd promised Ms. Shapiro would replace their paper clipboard, kept failing its tests, and he couldn't see why. He had written a Robot class the night before, private fields for team number and climb points, getter methods for each, everything wrapped neat and tidy the way the textbook said. Then the test, three lines long, had turned on him.

"Expected one hundred eighty," Michaela read over his shoulder, "but was zero. So your getter's broken." She pulled a folding chair up beside him and popped the tab on a can of soda that had clearly been shaken somewhere between the concession stand and the pit.

"That's the thing." James scrolled up through the code again. "It's not broken. Watch." He wrote a tiny main method, created a Robot, set its climb points, printed the value. One hundred eighty came out clean. The getter worked. He deleted the main method and ran the test again. Expected one hundred eighty, but was zero.

Aryana wandered over from the field, still holding the alliance selection sheet. "The app's dead, isn't it. We're going back to the clipboard." She said it lightly, but James heard the real question underneath, which was whether the two weeks he'd spent on this had been worth anything at all. Ms. Shapiro had told him before they left that failing in the pit was part of engineering, which was a colloquialism for we still expect results, and he'd nodded and not believed her.

"Give me ten minutes." He opened the test file and read it aloud, slowly, the way he'd taught himself to proofread essays. assertEquals, then one hundred eighty, then robot.getClimbPoints. "Wait." He looked at the failure message again. Expected one eighty, but was zero. If the expected value was one eighty, and the actual value was zero, then the getter was returning zero to the test but one eighty to his main method, which was impossible unless. He stopped. Unless the test's robot wasn't the robot he thought it was.

He scrolled to the setup method at the top of the file, the part he'd written at midnight and never reread, and there it was: the test robot was being constructed fresh for each test, and in one of them he was reading climb points before he'd ever set them. Zero was correct. Zero was the honest answer to a question he hadn't meant to ask. The confusing part was that the failure message said expected one hundred eighty, because in the method call, the expected value came first and the actual value came second, and he had been reading the message as if the world were the other way around. "The expected one goes first," he said, half to Michaela, half to the screen. "I had it backwards the whole time."

Michaela leaned in. "So the test was right and you were wrong."

"The test was right and I was wrong, and the message was telling me that in a language I didn't speak." It struck him as a pernicious little trap, honestly, because nothing crashed, nothing turned red in the editor, nothing said you have misunderstood the order of arguments. It just sat there and lied to him in perfect grammar. His old computer science teacher would have called this a learning experience. James called it three hours of his life, though he had to admit the hours had taught him something no lecture could, which was that a tool's failure message is written by someone who assumes you already understand the tool.

There was a twist still coming, and it arrived when Aryana, who had been reading his Robot class while they talked, tapped the screen. "Your setter for team number lets negatives through. Someone fat-fingers minus three and the whole sort breaks." She was right. He'd been so proud of the private fields, so sure that hiding the data was the whole point, that he'd forgotten the getters and setters were also a promise, a border where nonsense got turned away. Data that couldn't defend itself was data that could disenfranchise every team below it in a bad sort. He added a guard clause, one line, and wrote a new test for it, and this time he wrote the expected value first without thinking.

The loudspeaker called their match. Aryana stood, then paused. "So is it done?"

"It works," James said. "It works and it's wrong in at least three ways I haven't found yet." He closed the laptop and picked up the clipboard anyway, because the field came first. Michaela grabbed the Ethernet cable off the table and tossed it to him.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, which did not reveal that its author was a woman.
story:
The summer before college, Hailey was supposed to be reading nothing heavier than beach towels and departure boards, but her grandmother's bookcases had other plans. She had come to the house to help sort it for selling, three floors of furniture and smell of camphor, and on the second afternoon she opened a cabinet in the back parlour and found a row of clothbound books with spines gone soft as old fruit. One of them said Jane Eyre. She pulled it out because the name was familiar, because Professor Whatever in the fall syllabus had listed it, because her thumb wanted a reason to stop moving.

Inside, the title page did not say Charlotte Brontë. It said, in engraved letters, Jane Eyre: An Autobiography, edited by Currer Bell. She turned the page expecting the mistake to correct itself, an introduction, a note, something, but the book offered only the beginning of Jane's childhood and a girl shut in the red-room. She sat on the floor with the dust and texted Aikam, who was in the same first-year seminar and had already bought the annotated edition, the one with the essays in the back. "who is currer bell," she wrote. "is this like a fake editor or something." She could hear her mother downstairs wrapping dishes in newspaper, and her grandmother in the chair by the window saying, for the eleventh time, that nobody wanted the piano.

Aikam's answer arrived while Hailey was still squinting at the page. "Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell," he wrote. "didn't show she was a woman." Hailey read it twice, then looked at the book in her lap, at its plain brown boards, at the name that had done its work for a hundred and seventy years without her ever noticing. She thought of a boy in her AP class who had called something girly in that flattening tone, and how she had laughed, a small cowardly laugh she still remembered somatically, a tightening in the throat that came back now on the floor of the parlour.

"Come over," she texted. "bring your laptop. there's a thing here." He biked over within the hour because there was nothing else to do in the neighbourhood, and they sat at the kitchen table between boxed bowls while her grandmother dozed. The assignment, emailed early by the seminar professor, was to apply a critical lens to a passage from the novel, and Hailey had planned to do the feminist reading, the obvious one, the one she could do half asleep. But now she opened Aikam's copy to the passage where Jane is sent away to Lowood, and the two readings started fighting in her head. The girls at Lowood were stigmatized as unclean and unnatural, told to fast and be plain, and that was a feminist problem. But the men who ran the school also collected the donations, kept the porridge thin, and called luxury a sin for other people's children, and that was a Marxist one, and the two problems were not the same problem even though they lived in the same passage.

"Can you do both?" Aikam asked, spinning a teaspoon. "The prompt says a lens. Singular."

"Maybe that's the trap," Hailey said. "Pick one and pretend the other isn't there."

She typed a paragraph in which Jane's hunger was read twice, once as a woman's body disciplined into taking up less room, once as a child's labour cheapened by charity, and she could feel the two halves grinding against each other like unmatched gears. Then she deleted it, then she typed it again, then she deleted half of it. Her grandmother woke and shuffled in for water, saw the old book open on the table, and stood there a moment with her hand on its cover. "That was my mother's," she said. "She used to say Mr. Brocklehurst was a charlatan, a hypocrite who preached poverty from a nice house. I thought she was talking about her own minister." She laughed at the memory, or at something the memory had become, and went back to her chair.

Later, when the light had gone long and yellow across the boxes, Hailey still had not finished, and Aikam had fallen into the sofa with his shoes on, and the paragraph on the screen said everything she was sure of and nothing she wasn't. She wrote a sentence at the end admitting that she could not tell whether the mask of Currer Bell had freed the story or distorted it, whether a book that entered the world disguised as a man's editing could ever be read straight again, and she left it there, unresolved, because it was truer than a conclusion. She looked at the old volume, its author still hidden behind a name that had fooled her for two days and everyone else for a century, and she thought she had chosen her lens.

Then her grandmother called from the window chair, "Bring me that book before it gets packed. I want to read the end again, where Jane gets her inheritance." Hailey carried it over, and her grandmother opened it to the last chapters, and outside, faintly, the church bell rang the hour.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, which falls on April 4, 5 or 6, families visit their ancestors' graves to sweep and clean them and leave offerings of food.
story:
Carter had been to the church twice before his grandmother's funeral, once for a christening he could barely remember and once when the doors were open and he'd only gone in to get out of the rain. Now he sat in the third pew with his mother and his uncle, holding the order of service so hard the paper creased down the middle. His grandmother had never come here. She used to say the building was too quiet for her, that if God wanted to find her, God could come to the kitchen. Carter kept his eyes on the stained glass because it was easier than looking at the coffin, which was small in a way that didn't make sense.

The problem he could not solve was this: the funeral would end, everyone would eat sandwiches in the church hall, and then there would be nothing left to do. He had nothing scheduled with her anymore. No Sunday phone calls, no April trip to her apartment to help rotate the mattress. Grief kept handing him hours with nowhere to put them.

At the reception, Meganne found him by the tea urn. She had come even though she'd only met his grandmother once, at a school concert, and Carter was grateful in a way he didn't know how to say. "You look sullen," she said, which from her was not an insult, just an observation, the way she'd label a cloud type. He admitted he felt useless. He told her the thing about having nothing to do.

"That's the part my family fixed," Meganne said. "We're not like this church way, one day and it's over. Every spring, on the fourth, fifth or sixth of April, we go to the graves of our ancestors. We sweep them, we clean them, and we leave offerings of food." She stirred her tea. "It's called the Qingming Festival. My grandma says the food is for the dead, my dad says the food is for us, and they're both fine with that disagreement."

"The food is for us," Carter repeated.

"Whichever one you need it to be." She shrugged. "That's the whole trick, I think."

After the burial, the following weeks, Carter tried to acclimate himself to the ordinary shape of days. He went back to school. Cristiano saved him a seat in chemistry and didn't ask anything, which was its own kindness. But in April, on the fourth, which happened to fall on a Saturday, Carter woke early, took his mother's broom from the garage without asking, and put a plastic container of dumplings in his backpack. His grandmother had made them from a recipe on a package, badly, every winter, and he'd eaten them anyway. He'd bought frozen ones and microwaved them, and they were about as close as he could get.

The cemetery was a fifteen-minute walk. His uncle had warned him that the ground would still be cold and to wear boots, but nobody had warned him that cleaning a headstone would be so much work. There was a film of winter grit on the granite, and the grass at the base had been flattened by snow and needed raking with his fingers. He swept the stone itself in careful strokes, like the older man two rows over was doing with his family's plot, slow and thorough, not rushing. A groundskeeper slowed his truck to watch, then moved on. It took Carter nearly an hour, and the whole time he kept thinking that his effort wasn't for her exactly, but it wasn't not for her either, and both of those things could sit in the same hands holding the same broom.

He set the dumplings at the base of the stone. Then he sat down on the cold grass and ate two of them himself, because Meganne's family ate theirs too, and because he was hungry, and because it seemed right that the food should go both ways.

"Those look better than what we brought," said a voice. Ms. Yilmaz, his neighbour from three doors down, was standing at the next row with a cloth bag and a small rake. He hadn't known anyone in her family had died. She raised the bag slightly. "Apricots. My father's favourite. I do this every April, though I learned it from a friend, not from my own people." She looked at his broom, at the swept stone, at the container. "You didn't get that from your church."

"From Meganne," Carter said. "From her family, really. Her dad thinks the food is for the living, her grandma thinks it's for the dead."

Ms. Yilmaz considered this the way his chemistry teacher considered a hypothesis worth testing. "And you?"

"I haven't decided. I don't know if I have to." It sounded like dodging when he said it, but it wasn't; it was the most honest thing he'd worked out all month. He had taken somebody else's ritual because his own tradition had run out of instructions, and he couldn't tell yet whether that was borrowing or stealing or just being a person in the world with a broom.

He stood, brushed the grass off his jeans, and picked up the container to take the rest of the dumplings home. That was when he saw it: tucked against the back of the headstone, half hidden by the granite, a small orange, a boiled egg, and a note card in handwriting he recognized instantly, because he had seen it on birthday cards his whole life. His grandmother's handwriting. It was dated three years back. Someone had been leaving offerings here for years, before she was even buried here.

The card said, "For your father, Carter's great-grandfather. I'll keep coming. Love, G." Carter stood holding a container of microwave dumplings in front of a grave he had just cleaned, staring at an orange his dead grandmother had left for her dead father.

"Everything all right?" Ms. Yilmaz asked.

He looked at her, then at the orange, then at the road back toward his house.

"Did you leave the orange?" he said.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 13 in 100 people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy, mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time.
story:
Morgan had agreed to the peer-health training because Raphaelle had batted her eyelashes and promised free snacks, and now, on a Saturday she had meant to spend doing nothing at her grandmother's house, she found herself in the sunroom with a folder of pamphlets and an audience of two.

"We're the practice public," Spencer said, settling onto the wicker ottoman like a man about to watch something mildly embarrassing. "Do we get programs?"

"You get a laminated sheet." Raphaelle slid it across the tile floor with her foot. "Morgan, go. Consent first. Be effusive."

"I'm not supposed to be effusive, I'm supposed to be clear." Morgan stood, feeling ridiculous in front of the ferns and her grandmother's collection of decorative plates. "Okay. Consent. It has to be freely given, and it can be taken back at any time, even halfway through, even if you said yes an hour ago. If someone's been drinking, they can't really consent. And asking doesn't ruin the mood. Not asking does."

Spencer raised a hand. "Question from the public. What if the person is your lab partner and you're both awkward?"

"Then you use words, Spencer. Out loud. Astonishing, I know."

Her grandmother drifted through with a watering can, paused, and did not drift out again. Morgan's stomach tightened, but the old woman only said, "When I was young, nobody explained anything. My mother told me about a stork and left the room." She watered a plant that was clearly plastic. "Carry on."

Morgan turned the page. "Next: contraception. So, condoms. On the box they look basically bulletproof, right? Ninety-eight percent effective." She'd rehearsed this part in the mirror at home and had still gotten it wrong twice.

Spencer leaned forward. "Two failures out of a hundred. That's the number I've heard."

"That's perfect use," Morgan said. "But typical use, real people, a whole year relying only on male condoms? Thirteen in a hundred have an unintended pregnancy." She let that sit while Spencer's eyebrows climbed. "Mostly because condoms aren't used correctly every time. Not because the thing itself is a lottery."

"Thirteen," Spencer said, as if she'd accused him personally.

"Thirteen. Which is why the training says you lead with, don't rely on one method, use it right, every time. And honestly?" Morgan flipped her folder closed for a second. "Here's where I get stuck. Half the pamphlet is 'abstinence is the only hundred percent method,' and the other half is 'here's how to be safe if you're not abstinent.' And I think both are true at the same time, but I don't know how to say that to a room of fourteen-year-olds without sounding like a vending machine that can't decide."

"Say the true thing," her grandmother said from the doorway, apropos of nothing visible. "The true thing is usually two things."

"Thank you, Gran. Very helpful."

"You're welcome. There are biscuits."

Raphaelle pulled a biscuit from the tin that had appeared at Gran's elbow and held it up like a microphone. "Continue. Testing. This is the part where you pretend we're nervous."

Morgan took a breath. "Okay. Getting tested is routine. You can go to a clinic, you don't need a parent with you, and you can ask for a full panel even if you feel fine, because most infections don't announce themselves. It's mostly a urine sample or a swab, sometimes blood. Results in about a week. And if something comes back positive, most of it is treatable, and the clinic helps you tell partners without naming you if you don't want to."

"And if you're scared?"

"Then you bring a friend." Raphaelle pointed at herself. "Which is the actual reason I signed up. If anybody in that classroom is scared next year, in college, whenever, I want to be the person who'll sit in the waiting room with them and complain about the magazines."

The screen door clattered, and Mr. Nikolaidis from next door appeared with a plate of figs, an event so regular it counted as weather. "Am I interrupting a seance?"

"Health presentation," said Gran. "About condoms."

Mr. Nikolaidis, to his eternal credit, set down the figs, sat in the good chair, and said, "In my day the school showed us one filmstrip and propitiated our parents with a letter home. I don't think a single thing in the filmstrip was true. The letter, also doubtful."

"That's the patrimony we're trying to fix," Morgan said, surprising herself, "the inheritance of nobody telling anybody anything."

"Grand word." He took a fig. "Grand mostly because I never learned what to call it either."

Gran waters the plastic fern again on her way through, and Raphaelle laughs so hard she has to put the biscuit down, and Morgan, standing there with her folder, realizes she has stopped feeling ridiculous. Somewhere between the storks and the figs, the two halves of the pamphlet had stopped being a contradiction and started being one sentence, though she still couldn't write the sentence down. She looks at the empty doorway where Gran was, then at Spencer.

"Ask me the awkward lab partner question again," she says. "I think I have a better answer now."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: Putting another writer's idea into your own words still requires a citation, because plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording.
story:
Zachary spread the sources across the kitchen table after dinner, four books and a printed article, and opened a new document with his name and the date at the top. The assignment sheet from Ms. Ross lay beside the keyboard: eight pages, an argument, footnotes, a bibliography in a standard citation style. He had until Friday. He had never written anything longer than five pages, and those had been mostly summary, which Ms. Ross had underlined in red on his last essay with the single word "report" in the margin.

He began with the article, a chapter on urban renewal, and typed a paragraph about highway construction in the 1950s. Then he reread what he had written and realized it followed the article's order sentence by sentence, only in different words. He deleted it and tried again, breaking the ideas apart, putting the part about displaced residents first and the part about federal funding second. That was better. That was his own thinking, he decided, the shape of it at least. He kept going and by ten o'clock had two pages with no footnotes at all, because the footnotes, he reasoned, were for quotations, and he had quoted nothing.

At school the next morning he found Riley at the vending machines and said he was basically done with the draft already. Riley bought a bag of chips and said she was still on her sources. "I found this one book that says everything I want to say," she said, "so I'm, like, rewriting it in my own words. Ms. Ross can't complain because it's not copied." Zachary said that sounded right, and the bell rang, and they walked to class.

Ms. Ross kept them writing for the whole period and moved between the desks. When she stopped at Zachary's table she read his laptop screen for a long moment, then asked him to pull up his source list. He had three. His draft drew on five. "Where are the notes for the other two?" she asked, and he said he hadn't quoted them so he hadn't footnoted them. She looked at him, and then at the paragraph on displaced residents, and said, "Bring your sources tomorrow. We'll look together." She moved on before he could answer.

Riley, from two rows over, leaned into the aisle as Ms. Ross passed the window. "She said something like this last week," Riley said quietly. "Paraphrasing still needs a citation. Plagiarism isn't only copying exact wording, it's using ideas without credit." Zachary said he hadn't copied anything, and Riley said that wasn't the point, and turned back to her screen. Zachary sat with the sentence for the rest of the period, rereading his own paragraph, the one he had rearranged so carefully, seeing now that every fact in it had come from the article and none of it had come from him.

Riley watched him from across the room for the rest of the period. She had done the same thing herself two years earlier in her brother's old term paper file, a page with the margins full of a teacher's comments, and she remembered the specific humiliation of it, the way the teacher had interposed himself between her and her own draft as though she could not be trusted with it. She had wanted to say something to Zachary at the machines and had said it badly, making it sound like a loophole rather than a rule. She decided she would text him the writing center's webpage that night, and let the page do the rest.

At home that evening Zachary set the article beside his laptop and opened the guide to citation style that Ms. Ross had linked. He found the section on notes and bibliography and worked through the examples, then went back to his draft and inserted a footnote at the end of the highway paragraph. The note came out crooked, the author's name in the wrong order, and he fixed it against the model, then did the same for the next paragraph and the one after. It was slow. By nine o'clock the draft had eleven footnotes and the pages looked different to him, denser, more honest, argument and evidence visibly separate for the first time.

He kept thinking about what he had believed at the start, that changing the words made the idea his. It hadn't felt like chicanery at the time; it had felt like writing. That bothered him more than the mechanics did. He understood now that a citation was not an admission of weakness but a marker on a map, telling the reader which ground was his and which ground he was standing on that belonged to someone else. Whether his own argument, the thin thread of it running through the middle pages, was strong enough to carry any weight, he still could not tell, and he was honest enough with himself to leave that question open.

His mother came through the kitchen for a glass of water and stopped at the table. "This looks serious," she said.

"Footnotes," Zachary said. "I got it wrong for two pages and now I'm fixing it."

She looked over his shoulder at the small superscript numbers climbing the page. "It looks like a real paper now," she said, and he said, "It looks like one, anyway," and hit save.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: The US fairness doctrine, introduced in 1949, required broadcasters to air contrasting views on controversial public issues; the Federal Communications Commission abolished it in 1987.
story:
The group chat had been quiet all afternoon, and then Ross dropped the link at 4:47, right when Julia was supposed to be outlining her history essay. "Local paper says the mill closure is 'temporary,'" he typed. "My dad says it's permanent. They told the floor guys Monday." Below the link, a screenshot of the article, and below that, the byline: owned by Harrow Media Group, a name Julia had never thought about before, even though it ran in the corner of the site every time she looked up game scores.

"Who's Harrow?" she typed. Kobe answered fast, the way he did when he'd already been reading. "They own like forty papers. And the mill owes Harrow's bank a ton of money. My sister works there." Then he sent a shrug emoji and a single line: "Make of that what you want."

Julia made nothing of it, at first. She made dinner, which meant listening to her mother rehearse complaints about the mill, and then she carried her phone to the living room where her grandfather was watching the news with the sound low. She asked him, almost as a joke, whether the paper had always been like this. He turned the sound off entirely.

"Used to be a rule," he said. "Fairness doctrine. Nineteen forty-nine. TV stations had to air contrasting views on controversial public issues. Both sides, whether they liked it or not." He scratched his jaw. "FCC abolished it in eighty-seven. Before you were born." She asked what the FCC was and he just pointed at the screen, as if the government lived somewhere inside it, and went back to his program. She stood there a moment, then took her phone to the kitchen and looked it up herself, because that was the only way she trusted anything now.

The chat was alive when she got back. Ross had found a Harrow paper in another town, three years back, that had called a similar closure "a pause" right up until the demolition. Kobe had found a statement from the paper's editor saying coverage was independent, full stop. "So which is it," Ross typed, and then, before anyone could answer: "They can both be true, right? It can be independent and still slanted. Nobody has to order anybody around."

Julia started typing three different replies and deleted each one. The first was too much like Kobe's sister, gossip dressed as proof. The second was a kind of syllogism, she realized, all premises and a conclusion, and conclusions were exactly what she didn't have. The third was just "idk," which was true but useless. She typed instead: "My grandpa says stations used to have to show both sides. They don't anymore. So now we check." Ross sent back a single word: "check what."

That was the question, and she sat on the kitchen stool with her thumb hovering, actually thinking about how you would check. The mill's own filings, maybe. The union's page. The paper's past stories lined up beside what had actually happened later. She was aware that her whole method was embryonic, a few limbs and no spine, and that Kobe's sister's salary and Ross's dad's anger were also facts, also parts of the animal. She said none of this. She sent: "the paper's other closures. What they said then. What happened after."

Mr. Njoroge, who coached her debate team and lurked in the chat without ever commenting, sent his first message in four months: a thumbs up. Kobe followed with the archive link to the other Harrow paper, the one from three years ago, and Julia opened it and started reading the old headlines in order, September through June, "pause," "pause," "pause," "redevelopment opportunity." She screenshotted the sequence and held her thumb over the send button, because the screenshots didn't exonerate anybody, they didn't prove the editor was lying or owned, they only showed what a paper had chosen to call a thing while the thing came down.

Ross was already typing. Kobe was already typing. She could see both bubbles pulsing under the thread, two answers being built at the same time, and she sent the screenshots before either one arrived.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Cocoa butter can crystallize in six different forms, and tempering aims to make most of it set in form V, the crystal form that gives shine and snap.
story:
Chloe told herself she wasn't nervous, which was the first lie of the afternoon, because her hands were already sweating and she hadn't even picked up the spatula yet. The community kitchen on Delancey Street smelled of onions from the morning soup crew, and under that, faintly, of the chocolate Ms. Nur kept locked in the pantry for the Saturday class. Chloe had failed twice at home. Both batches had set dull as river stones, crumbling when she broke them, and she had eaten the evidence alone at the counter so her mother wouldn't ask questions. Today she intended to find out why.

"You're staring at the couverture like it insulted you," Jacey said, tying her apron.

"It kind of did." Chloe chopped the block into even pieces, the knife ticking against the board. Frederik arrived late, hair wet from the rain, and Ms. Nur set a folded towel beside his station without a word, so he wouldn't have to ask for one. Chloe noticed that. She noticed most things, though she rarely said so, and she had decided last week that noticing was her way of caring, which was easier than the other ways.

Ms. Nur wrote the temperatures on the whiteboard: melt, cool, rewarm, and a small window where the chocolate had to be worked. "The chocolate will tell you when it's ready," she said. "It stops being willing." She would not say more. She believed, Chloe had gathered, that explanations handed over were explanations not owned.

So Chloe worked it out herself, or tried to. She melted the chocolate to the number on the board, poured two-thirds of it onto the marble slab that Ms. Nur kept in the freezer, and began spreading and scraping it with the palette knife. The sound changed as it cooled, from a loose slosh to something with a body to it. Her arms ached. Jacey, watching, slid a stool over so Chloe could rest a hip against it, and took over the scraping for a minute without being asked, handing the knife back at exactly the moment Chloe's grip said she wanted it.

Frederik leaned over his own bowl, frowning. "Mine looks like mud."

"Mine looked like mud on Tuesday," Chloe said. "I read about it. Cocoa butter can crystallize in six different forms." She kept folding, watching the gloss begin to rise on the marble like a slow tide. "Tempering is basically herding it into form V. That's the crystal form that gives shine and snap."

"Form five," Frederik repeated, as if testing whether the words held weight.

"Form V," Chloe corrected, and grinned at him. "Everything else is the mud."

She added the reserved warm chocolate back in, rewarming the mass, and the shine held, trembling, not quite solid and not quite liquid. Here was where her thinking divided, and she let the two halves argue while her hands kept moving. One half of her wanted to be the autocrat of the bowl, to force the temperature into compliance, to control everything down to the degree, because control had kept her steady through her parents' year of low voices behind doors. The other half had learned, somewhere between the first failed batch and this one, that the chocolate could not be commanded, only persuaded. Cocoa butter would crystallize however it chose unless you gave it a reason, and even then it only mostly obeyed. Mostly. She was honest enough with herself to admit that mostly bothered her, that she wanted the six forms sorted into ranks, the good crystal guaranteed. The science gave her a window, not a promise.

She tested it the way the book said: dipped the tip of a knife and waited. In her kitchen at home this moment had gone wrong twice, and both times she had told herself the batch was fine, really, that dullness was only an aesthetic problem. She knew now that the lie was a habit, that she narrated her own failures into smallness so they'd fit inside her. The knife tip set in under two minutes, glossy.

She poured into the molds Jacey had lined up, tapping each one against the counter to chase the bubbles out. Frederik hovered. "If mine doesn't work, can I have some of yours?"

"You can have some of mine either way," Chloe said, and meant it.

While the molds sat in the cool room, she scraped the bowl with a spoon and ate what remained, standing at the sink, and thought about the two ways of holding a thing: gripping it or keeping your hands open under it. She could not claim she'd chosen, only that she'd felt both at once, and that maybe a considered position was less a decision than a truce. Her nascent theory, untested, was that most people were like cocoa butter, settling into whatever shape the temperature of a room allowed, and that the work of a person was to notice which form she was in before it hardened.

Twenty minutes later she unmolded the first bar by flipping the plastic and rapping it once. The chocolate dropped out dark and glassy. She snapped a corner off and the sound was clean, like a small branch breaking in dry air. Frederik's bar came out matte, and he groaned, and Chloe slid her bar across the counter to him without ceremony.

"Break it again," she said. "Louder this time."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA advises reheating leftovers to an internal temperature of 74 degrees Celsius (165 degrees Fahrenheit).
story:
Kaitlyn had, in her own considered opinion, an unshakable head under pressure, which is why she'd volunteered to run the meal-prep program at Ms. Somsak's restaurant while the regular cook recovered from knee surgery. All she had to do was plan seven dinners for the family, shop for the ingredients on a budget Ms. Somsak had written on a napkin, and cook everything in batches on Sundays so her mother could reheat a container each night after her shift. Simple. She had made a spreadsheet. The spreadsheet had color coding. Nothing about a spreadsheet with color coding had ever gone wrong.

"Nothing about a spreadsheet has ever gone wrong," she told Arman on Saturday, holding her phone up in the dry goods aisle of the grocery store like a lantern.

Arman looked at the list, then at the cart, then at her. "We have forty pounds of rice."

"We have ten."

"Kaitlyn. I'm looking at ten bags of rice that each weigh four pounds."

"That's the bulk discount," she said, which was true, and also not what she'd meant to buy, and she decided not to dwell on it. Beside the rice sat a recalcitrant butternut squash that refused to fit anywhere in the cart and had to ride on top of the napkins like a figurehead. Tyler met them at the register, having been sent to "supervise," and spent the whole checkout making the squash narrate its feelings in a small tragic voice. By the time they got back to the restaurant kitchen, Kaitlyn was almost too delighted to notice they'd forgotten the chicken.

Almost.

Sunday arrived with the smell of onions going soft in butter, six quarts of rice steaming in the big pot, and the chicken, retrieved by Tyler at a run, browning in strips. Ms. Somsak drifted through now and then to check the soup, because the kitchen was still, technically, open for lunch prep. Kaitlyn portioned everything into containers, labeled them with the days of the week, and stacked them in the walk-in like a small city of leftovers. She was, she reminded herself, extremely calm. Her heart, which had begun to palpitate somewhere around the second batch of rice, was merely enthusiastic.

Then she found the note taped to the walk-in door, in Ms. Somsak's round, unhurried handwriting: "Kaitlyn. Batch cooking is a wonderful skill. So is the thermometer, which lives in the drawer by the sink and which you have not used once today. Reheated food has rules. Ask the thermometer, not your eyes. It will not lie to you, which is more than I can say for some spreadsheets I have seen. P.S. The chicken smells good. Do not poison my Tuesday."

Kaitlyn read it twice. In her opinion, the food looked fine, smelled fine, and was fine, and she said so to the drawer while taking out the thermometer anyway. It was a slim metal probe with a dial like a tiny clock. She pulled the Wednesday container back out of the walk-in, scooped a mound of rice into a bowl, and microwaved it until steam rose off it in a convincingly dinner-like way. The rice looked done. The rice looked beyond suspicion.

The thermometer said sixty-two degrees Celsius. She squinted at the dial. There was a small arrow pointing to one hundred and sixty-five, which was, according to the little chart on the thermometer's casing, one hundred and sixty-five degrees Fahrenheit, and also, in smaller print, seventy-four degrees Celsius. The needle was nowhere near the arrow.

"Arman," she called across the kitchen. "Come be a witness."

"To what?"

"To me being right about rice." She stirred the bowl, microwaved it another minute, and stabbed the probe back into the center. Seventy-one. Another minute, a stir, the probe again, and finally the needle climbed to seventy-four degrees Celsius, one hundred and sixty-five Fahrenheit, exactly on the arrow, and Kaitlyn exhaled a breath she had not, in her own telling, been holding. She texted her mother a photo of the thermometer with the caption "USDA says 74C or 165F for reheating leftovers, we are OFFICIALLY edible," and her mother replied with three thumbs-up and a picture of the cat.

She thought about it while she scrubbed the rice pot. On one hand, she had always trusted her eyes, and her eyes had never, as far as she knew, poisoned anyone; on the other hand, the thermometer had just shown her a bowl of steaming, innocent-looking rice that was eleven degrees shy of legal. Perhaps the truth was that both were useful and only one of them could be argued with. She hadn't decided yet whether the extra minutes of microwaving were worth it for food that was probably fine anyway, and she suspected Ms. Somsak would say the word "probably" belonged in a swamp, not a kitchen.

Ms. Somsak came through at closing, lifted a container, and weighed it in her hand like a piece of fruit. "This is Tuesday's recompense for a week of your mother not having to cook," she said, and handed it to Kaitlyn with the formality of someone awarding a medal. "The chicken?"

"Forgot it, ran for it, browned it, thermometed it," Kaitlyn said. "There's a chart. There's an arrow. The arrow and I are close now."

Tyler, elbow-deep in dishwater, held up the squash, which had survived the weekend on the counter. "He wants to know if he's Thursday."

"He's Thursday," Kaitlyn said, and peeled back the lid to smell the chicken one more time, just in case her eyes knew something after all.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: A blind spot is an area around a car the driver cannot see from the seat, even with mirrors, which is why drivers turn their heads to check before changing lanes.
story:
The key to the Beatrice Street cul-de-sac, Mr. Ivanova said, was to take it slowly, and Thomas took him at his word, easing the car out of the driveway with the caution of a man defusing something. Mr. Ivanova had taught drivers for thirty years, though he no longer advertised; he did it now for neighbours' children, for something to do, for the pleasure, Thomas suspected, of sitting beside seventeen-year-olds at the exact moment they discovered that a steering wheel was not a toy. Gideon had wedged himself into the back seat, ostensibly for moral support, actually to narrate.

"Release the brake more," Mr. Ivanova said. "You're driving like you're apologizing to the car."

Thomas laughed, and the laugh loosened something in his shoulders, and the car rolled down Kestrel Road at a speed that felt enormous to him and funereal to everyone else. The street was quiet in the way of a Sunday morning: sprinklers ticking, a man across the road washing a bicycle with a sponge, the light through the maples coming down in coins on the windshield. Thomas had spent months imagining this, and now that it was happening it kept sliding sideways from what he'd pictured. In his imagination driving was freedom, an epigram his uncle liked, something about the open road. On Kestrel Road it was closer to arithmetic: pedal, mirror, wheel, and a fear of the parked cars that felt personally directed at him.

"Take us out to Marsh Lane," Mr. Ivanova said, and Marsh Lane meant leaving the suburbs, which meant the road with two lanes going their way. Thomas signalled, checked the mirror, and began to drift left. Gideon, from behind, said "Whoa," in a flat voice, the kind of whoa that carries information, and Mr. Ivanova said "Stop," not loudly, and Thomas stopped, and there in the lane beside them, close enough to touch, was a silver hatchback that had come from nowhere, that had been there the whole time.

"Where did he come from?" Thomas said. His hands were sweating through the wheel.

"He was always there," Gideon said. "Blind spot. The mirrors don't show you everything, so you've got to actually turn your head." He said it in the tone of someone reciting something he'd been told, and Thomas realized Gideon's mother had been drilling him for months, since before either of them had permits.

Mr. Ivanova said only, "Again, when you're ready." Thomas signalled again, turned his head properly this time, an odd theatrical gesture that felt wrong and was right, saw the empty lane behind his shoulder, and moved over. The car crossed the dotted line smoothly, and Mr. Ivanova made an effusive noise of approval, one short syllable that from him amounted to a standing ovation. Thomas felt a flash of pride, and then, under it, something less pleasant: the understanding that the pride was built on a near miss, that if Gideon had been looking at his phone instead of out the window, the silver car would have been a problem he solved by collision. Everything he was learning seemed underpinned like that, by the accidents that almost happened, the invisible cars riding along beside him.

They did three more lane changes, then the turn back onto Kestrel Road, then the slow ceremonial creep up his own driveway, and Mr. Ivanova said it had been a good first lesson, genuinely good, and Gideon got out and stretched like a man leaving a long flight. Thomas sat for a second in the driver's seat after the engine died, still holding the wheel, and Gideon leaned in through the open door.

"Can I get a ride to school tomorrow?"

"You know I can't drive without a licensed adult."

"Right, right," Gideon said, already backing away, grinning. "You're the one who can drive now. I'll just ride the bus."

Mr. Ivanova pocketed the keys and started down the sidewalk toward his own house, and Thomas watched him go, then got out and stood for a moment in the driveway, looking up the empty street where the silver hatchback would never know how close it had come to mattering.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: Peak bone mass is typically reached in the early twenties in women and the late twenties in men, so bone built in the teenage years affects bone strength for life.
story:
Sara found her grandmother at the kitchen table on Tuesday morning, sitting with her leg stretched out and a folder of hospital papers beside the teapot. The hip had broken three weeks earlier, on the second stair of her own porch, and now she had moved in temporarily, filling the house with the smell of menthol and the sound of daytime television nobody watched.

"You look like her," her grandmother said, meaning Sara's mother, though Sara suspected she was really stalling. "Sit. Tell me about this test."

The test was the problem. The university Sara would start at in September required a fitness assessment for anyone joining the varsity track team, and hers was scheduled for the last Friday in August, eleven days before move-in. She had signed up in a fit of ambition in spring, when the whole thing had felt abstract, like a country she might visit. Now it was a country with a border crossing, and she had spent the summer doing almost nothing, telling herself that walking to work counted, that she would start next week, that next week always existed.

"I'm going to withdraw my registration," she said.

Her grandmother reached for the folder, and Sara saw her wince, the whole right side of her tightening around the hip the way a hand tightens around something fragile. Inside the folder were discharge instructions, a physiotherapy schedule, and, inexplicably, an old affidavit from 1987, signed by a lawyer Sara had never heard of, certifying something about a property line. Her grandmother kept her papers together without system, as if document and document might keep each other company.

"I broke it because it was weak," her grandmother said, not looking up. "The doctor was very cheerful about it. Apparently that is common."

That afternoon Dorothy came over, ostensibly to study for their online course in personal finance, actually to eat Sara's mother's biscotti and complain. The course was Dorothy's idea of a career plan; she had already decided she would monetize a channel about budgeting, filming herself at the grocery store comparing unit prices, though so far she had four subscribers, three of whom were Sara under different accounts.

"I don't get why you'd quit," Dorothy said, feet on the chair rungs. "You ran all through grade eleven. You were good."

"I was good then. Now I'd have to train for eleven days to be mediocre, and probably injure myself, and start school on crutches."

Kelly-Ann arrived at six with her laptop, because she was the one among them who actually read things. She had heard about the grandmother, and while the older woman dozed in the armchair, Kelly-Ann looked up bone density on a whim, the way she looked up everything, and read aloud in her flat reporting voice.

"Peak bone mass is typically reached in the early twenties in women and the late twenties in men. So bone built in the teenage years affects bone strength for life."

Sara said nothing at first. In the armchair her grandmother's eyes were closed, and Sara watched her breathe, and thought about the second stair of a porch, thirty or forty or fifty years away, and whether the person climbing it was being decided now, this August, in this kitchen. It seemed both absurd and unarguable, the way compound interest had seemed in the finance course until Dorothy showed her the spreadsheet.

The next morning Sara set her alarm for six and ran to the park and back, four kilometres that felt like eight. She did it again Thursday, and Friday she found the dusty weights in the basement and lifted them badly, then watched a video and lifted them less badly. Her mother's boyfriend, a choleric man who coached a junior soccer league and shouted at referees from the couch, noticed by Sunday and offered unsolicited advice about interval training, which Sara took as a sign of how visible her effort had become.

"You're doing this for a test," her grandmother said on Wednesday, watching Sara stretch in the living room. "I did nothing for anything. I was busy. Everyone is always busy."

"It's not just the test anymore," Sara said, and found that she meant it, though she could not have said exactly what it was for, whether for the stairs of some future porch or for the plain animal pleasure of her legs working again, or for the version of herself who had signed up in spring and deserved an answer. She was honest enough to admit she did not know which, and that the not knowing did not seem to stop it mattering.

On the last Friday in August she took the bus to the university's athletic centre, changed in the echoing locker room, and ran the assessment on the indoor track while a bored student assistant clicked a stopwatch. She finished the distances respectably, not brilliantly, and walked out into the hot parking lot already planning Tuesday's run.

Her phone buzzed before she reached the bus stop. It was her mother. The university had emailed; the assessment had been rescheduled to October due to facility maintenance, and her registration, somehow, had never gone through in the first place.

Sara stood holding the phone, sweat cooling on her neck, and then she laughed, alone, in the parking lot, and started to jog home.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Each transfer RNA carries one amino acid and has a three-base anticodon that pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA.
story:
The retake was scheduled for Friday, and Mr. Paquette had made the terms clear: Nolan could sit the transcription and translation quiz again only if he first taught the material to someone else, out loud, without notes. "You understand it when you can make another person understand it," Mr. Paquette had said, in that flat way he had, which Nolan had once imputed to indifference until he realized it was patience, worn thin from repetition. Either way the condition stood, and Nolan had three days to turn a memorized jumble of codons and polymerases into something he could actually hand to another human being.

He recruited Walter and Angus, who agreed on the condition that they could film the whole thing on Walter's phone, a stipulation Nolan accepted because he had no leverage. They took over the community garden behind the science wing during last period study hall, a rectangle of raised beds where the tenth graders grew lettuce nobody ate. Nolan spread a deck of index cards across the picnic table. Some cards were blank strips marked with three letters, codons he had copied from the whiteboard that morning. Others were folded into paper loops, each one labelled on the outside with three letters and on the inside with an amino acid name.

"So we're the cell," Angus said, picking up a card and smelling it suspiciously.

"You're the messenger RNA," Nolan said. "You're the strip. You just stand there and hold your codons out." He handed Walter a paper loop. "You're a transfer RNA. You carry one amino acid. Just one, that's the whole job. One loop, one amino acid." Walter unfolded his loop, read the inside, and shrugged. "And you match yourself to him," Nolan went on, pointing at Angus. "Your three letters pair with his three letters. Three against three. That's how you know where to hand it over."
