They ran it once and it failed immediately, and the failure was interesting. Walter had grabbed two loops at once, one in each hand, reasoning that a courier would obviously carry as much cargo as possible. Nolan stopped the filming and stood there in the cold air feeling the shape of his own mistake from the morning quiz. He had thought of the transfer RNAs as generic delivery guys, interchangeable little trucks, when really each one was a specific key: three letters on the outside, one amino acid hidden on the inside, and no flexibility about either. "You can't carry two," he said slowly. "Put one down." It wasn't that he had been told this and forgotten it. It was that he had never quite believed it until he watched Walter standing there, overfull, obviously wrong.

Walter dropped the second loop into the lettuce bed and lined up against Angus, holding his card out like a badge. "AUG," Angus read off the strip. Walter turned his loop around and they matched letters, three to three, and Walter handed over the amino acid written inside. "That's it," Nolan said. "That's translation. That exact thing, like four hundred thousand times." Angus wrote the amino acid name in his notebook, becoming, by mutual agreement, the growing protein chain. He added a small flourish after each name, a mannerism he'd picked up from some detective show, and Nolan let it go because it was not germane to the mechanism and because Angus was doing it free of charge.

They filmed nine takes. Between takes, Nolan kept noticing things he couldn't have listed from the textbook but which the cards made obvious: that the messenger RNA didn't do anything except be read, that the matching was all in the letters, that the protein's identity came entirely from the order of handoffs. Change one letter on one loop and you'd deliver the wrong amino acid and get a wrong protein. He didn't say any of this out loud. He just stood by the lettuce with his hands in his pockets, turning it over, wondering whether the cell ever got deliveries out of order, and whether it mattered, and deciding that these were questions for after Friday.

On Friday morning Walter texted him the video, unedited, eleven minutes long, mostly Angus dramatically accepting amino acids. Nolan watched it twice on the bus, then a third time with his eyes closed, listening to his own voice say the words. Each transfer RNA carries one amino acid, and it has an anticodon, three letters, that pairs with the matching three letters on the messenger RNA. He had said it so many times on camera that it had stopped sounding like a sentence and started sounding like the thing itself, small and exact and relentless.

Mr. Paquette set the retake on his desk and watched Nolan read the first question. Nolan's pen hovered, then moved. Outside the window, the tenth graders were back at the lettuce beds, and someone was holding up a card to the light, squinting at it from both sides.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech; it does not by itself stop a private employer or private company from restricting speech.
story:
The courthouse steps were still warm at four in the afternoon, and Addison sat on the second one from the bottom with her brief folded in quarters, reading the same paragraph for the fifth time. Inside, Judge Marlow's courtroom had been assigned to the regional mock court, and tomorrow she would stand at the podium and argue Cruz's side, then turn around and argue against it, twenty minutes total, on a case about whether a private political forum could ban a user for his posts.

"I don't get how you argue both sides," Said said, dropping down beside her with two bottles of water from the machine. "Isn't one of them wrong?"

"That's the assignment," Addison said. "You get a better score if the judges can't tell which side you actually believe."

Said unwrapped a straw with more violence than the straw required. "Then what do you believe? Because yesterday in the van you said Cruz's rights were violated, and Solomon nearly climbed over the seat."

Solomon was leaning against the railing a few steps up, and he didn't pretend not to hear. "I said his free speech rights weren't violated, because the website isn't the government. I said it twice, actually."

"You said it like a rule you memorized," Addison said, and heard how defensive it came out, so she softened it. "The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech. It doesn't stop a private company from restricting it. That's what you said, and I wrote it down, and I've been trying to break it all night."

Mr. Sun, who coached the team and taught civics in a town forty minutes away, had driven the van and now came out the heavy doors with the schedule sheet in one hand. He did not sit, which meant he was about to hand down something. "The judges tomorrow are two attorneys and a real appellate clerk. They will ask about standing, about state action, and at least one of them will use the word germane. Make sure your answers are."

"Everything in my brief is germane," Addison said.

"Then you're the first student in ten years of whom that's true." He handed her the sheet and went to move the van, and his footsteps echoed off the stone in a way that made the whole building sound older than it was.

She spread the brief on the step and the paper caught a little wind, so Solomon put his own bottle on the corner of it without being asked. "Here's my problem," she said. "If I only argue your side, I win on the law. Cruz posted on a private site, the site removed him, the First Amendment doesn't apply. Clean. But then the judges ask me why we're all so upset about it, and I don't have a law for that part, just a feeling."

"That's because it isn't a legal question," Solomon said.

"It might be half of one." She was thinking out loud now, watching a sparrow work the mortar between two blocks of limestone. "The company can restrict his speech. Nothing stops it. But nothing stops the state legislature either, if it wants to pass some rule about platforms. So the interesting question isn't whether Cruz has a First Amendment claim against the website. He doesn't. It's whether the First Amendment limits what the government can do when it tries to make private companies carry speech they don't want." She looked up. "Is that allowed? Regulating the regulator?"

Said stopped chewing his straw. "You just turned Solomon's point into your closing argument."

"I turned it into both of them." She was gesticulating with the rolled schedule now, pointing at the courthouse doors as if the courtroom itself were the opposing counsel. "For Cruz I concede the whole first half. Yes, the First Amendment limits the government, not the website. I stipulate it in my first sentence. And then I say: the question before this court isn't what the company may do, it's what the state may do to the company. For the other side, I argue the legislature did nothing to the company's speech, only to its advertising, and the district court said that's a distinction, and I'm not sure the district court is right, but I'm not required to be sure, I'm required to argue it."

Solomon had moved down a step during all this, which he did when something interested him. "Yesterday you told me the case was about a man being silenced."

"Yesterday I hadn't read the cases you photocopied." She said it without apology, and he nodded slowly, the way he nodded at a chess move he hadn't considered.

The light was going amber on the pillars by the time they went back inside to find the practice room. In the corridor outside Courtroom 2, a security officer asked them to sign in, and Addison noticed the pen was chained to the desk, a small government solution to a small private temptation, and she filed the observation away without deciding what it meant. She took the podium in the empty practice room, set her brief on it, and began to speak to the folding chairs.

"May it please the court. My client's speech was restricted, and the First Amendment, which limits what the government may do to speech, offers him no remedy against the private company that restricted it. I will not pretend otherwise."

The chairs said nothing. Solomon, in the front row with his arms crossed, uncrossed them.

"So I ask the court to look one step further up, at the state that leaned on the company, at the question underneath the question. And I'd like to begin with the facts."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A table read is a seated read-through of a script by the cast, used to hear how the dialogue sounds before any staging begins.
story:
Eve had pushed the coffee table to the middle of the living room and set four chairs around it, which was as close to a theatre as the house got on a Tuesday afternoon. Her script lay in front of the seat she had decided was hers, though she had not sat in it yet. She kept finding reasons to stand: refilling the water glasses, straightening the stack of pages, checking that the door to the hallway was closed so her mother would not wander through in her socks.

"It's called a table read," Musa said, arranging his pages against the table's edge. "A seated read-through of the script by the cast. You use it to hear how the dialogue sounds before you do any staging." He said it the way he said most things he had learned that week, plainly, as though handing her a tool.

Rylee arrived with her shoes already off, holding a bag of clementines, and Mr. Taylor, who had agreed to read the mother because Eve could not ask her actual mother, took the fourth chair and folded his reading glasses open. Eve finally sat. She had written a ten-minute play about the night her grandmother moved into the care home, and she had chosen it because it was small enough to hold and true enough to matter, and now the two of those qualities seemed to be at war.

She had underwritten the whole thing herself, in the sense that she had quietly paid for it: the ream of paper, the evening she should have spent on calculus, the risk of showing the plainest thing she owned to three people who knew her. Mr. Taylor asked if she wanted to say anything first. She said no, start on page one, and put her hands flat on her knees.

The play opened with the daughter, based on Eve, carrying a box of photographs into an empty room. Rylee read the daughter's lines. She read them well, in fact, with a softness Eve had not written, and for the first page and a half Eve felt the odd consonance of hearing words she had only ever heard inside her own head now spoken in someone else's voice, the two sounds agreeing with each other the way two notes in tune agree.

Then the mother spoke, and Eve's stomach dropped. The line was "I raised you to be better than a woman who cries in parking lots." Rylee said it, then stopped, and looked up over the page. In Eve's head the line had been devastating. In the living room it was nothing, worse than nothing; it sounded like a line, a phrase manufactured to be devastating, and no one at that table believed a real mother had ever said it. Musa cleared his throat and turned the page too early.

"Keep going," Eve said, and they did, and she took notes on the back of an envelope, but the notes were mostly one word repeated: false, false, false. The grandmother's actual last words in that real parking lot had been "Did you bring the good scissors?" said in a tone that had frightened Eve more than any accusation could have, because it was calm, and small, and aimed at nothing. Eve had not put that line in the play. She had replaced it with something bigger because the true thing had seemed too small to carry the scene.

They finished the read-through. Mr. Taylor peeled a clementine and said the mother needed a smaller cutlery drawer of a part, fewer things but sharper ones, and Musa said the middle went quiet, and Rylee said the grandmother was the best person on the page and she was barely in it. Eve listened with the envelope against her knee. She understood, sitting there, that the table read had done exactly what it was for: it had let her hear the dialogue before anyone staged anything, before she wasted a single rehearsal defending lines that could not survive being said out loud.

She crossed out the manufactured line and wrote the true one above it, then read it aloud herself, testing it. "Did you bring the good scissors?" The room went still in a way it had not gone still all afternoon. Rylee nodded slowly. Musa said the grandmother should say it twice, once at the start and once near the end, the second time when nobody had asked about scissors at all, and Eve wrote that down too, though she was not certain yet whether repetition would deepen the moment or just explain it. She was not certain about several things: whether her mother could ever sit through this play, whether small was the same as true, whether she had the right to put a real woman's confusion on a stage for strangers. She looked at the three faces around the table, still waiting, the pages soft in their hands.

"Once more," Eve said, "from the top."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Psychologist Robert Zajonc's 1968 experiments showed the mere-exposure effect: people tend to like things more simply because they have seen them more often.
story:
Audrey kept her palm flat on the cardboard box between her feet so it wouldn't slide when her mother took the highway ramp too fast. The box held the important things, or the things she had decided, at two in the morning with tape in her teeth, were important: three photographs, a mug from Zakaria with a chip in the rim, and her psychology notes from second semester, which she was not bringing to study so much as to hold.

"Forty more minutes," her mother said, though Audrey had counted the exits herself and it was closer to seventy. Her mother had been rounding down all summer, as if the move could be made smaller by arithmetic.

The flashcards were on top of the notes because Ms. Leblanc had made them copy the studies out by hand, which Audrey had thought was punishment at the time. She lifted the rubber band off and fanned through them. Milgram. Asch. Then the one she was looking for, though she hadn't known she was looking. Zajonc, 1968. People tend to like things more simply because they have seen them more often.

She put it back without reading further. She didn't want that one. She wanted the mug, wanted Zakaria's loud laugh in the stairwell of the old school, wanted Zaid saving her a seat in the cafeteria by balancing his water bottle on the chair like a flag planted in claimed territory. The last week, Zaid had actually offered to drive the six hours to visit her in October, and she had said yes, and she had meant it, and she had also thought, privately and with some shame, that by October he would have forgotten, and that this was fine, because she might have forgotten too.

"It's called the mere-exposure effect," Zakaria had told her in June, the last week of school, when she'd been complaining about the new town. She'd visited once, in March, and hated everything about it, most of all the bus route her mother had mapped from the new house to the new school, which looped through an industrial park for no reason Audrey could see. "Zajonc, 1968," Zakaria had said, tapping her notes. "You like stuff more just from seeing it more. It's the whole reason advertising works. Give it a month and you'll probably like that lugubrious bus route." He'd been joking, and she'd thrown a balled-up napkin at him across the cafeteria table, and Ms. Leblanc had passed by and said nothing, only moved a glass of water away from the notes, a small mercy that Audrey had noticed and not thanked her for.

Now, forty-one minutes in, her mother said, "You could call Zaid tonight." Audrey said the chargers were in the other box. This was a lie, and she knew it was a lie, and the strange thing was that she said it anyway, cleanly, without guilt arriving until the next exit. She had been telling herself for weeks that she was leaving because the family was leaving, which was true, and that she had no choice, which was also true, and underneath both of these a quieter story ran: that she was relieved. That the relief was so large it frightened her, a kind of exhilaration she couldn't say out loud because it would make her a bad friend, and so she had been performing grief instead, carefully, for an audience of people who loved her.

She took out the flashcard again. She read it all the way through this time. If Zakaria was right, then whatever she hated about the new town, the bus route, the industrial park, the strange smell near the culvert, would wear smooth like river stone just by being seen day after day. And if that was true, then her grief might atrophy the same way. She tested the idea from both directions, holding it the way Ms. Leblanc had taught them to hold a study, asking what it predicted and what it left out. It predicted she would come to like the new town, given time. It did not predict whether that would be a small happiness or a kind of forgetting. She could not tell, from the card, whether she was being offered comfort or a warning, and she was honest enough with herself, at least alone in a moving car, to sit with not knowing.

They pulled into a gas station on the edge of the new town, the last one before the exit, and her mother said, "Bathroom break, then we're home." Home. Audrey carried the box to the picnic table beside the pumps, set it down, and took out her phone. Nine percent battery. She scrolled to Zaid's name and looked at it while a truck growled past on the road behind her. Then she typed, "I'm here. It's ugly. Ask Zakaria what the flashcard says about that," and pressed send before she could revise it into something safer. Outside the window of the station's little shop, she could see the industrial park's water tower, silver and ridiculous against the flat sky, and she found she was already half-smiling at it, and she noticed that too.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: The 'file drawer problem', a term coined by psychologist Robert Rosenthal in 1979, describes studies with null results going unpublished, which makes the published record look more positive than the evidence.
story:
Jayden had spread the two articles across the kitchen table like playing cards he didn't trust. One, from a team in Toronto, claimed that later school start times raised attendance measurably. The other, a single author writing out of Cardiff, had found almost no effect and said so in a paragraph so dry it read like an apology. The assignment, printed and pinned under his water glass, asked him to compare the two and take a position. He had a bowl of cereal, a highlighter bleeding orange onto his thumb, and no position.

His father passed through on his way to the printer, where a renewal notice was waiting. "Three hundred more this year," the dad said. "They indemnify the car, they indemnify the house, and every year it costs more to be protected from exactly the same things." He waved the pages at Jayden as though Jayden had set the price himself.

Jayden nodded without looking up. The Toronto article was polished, confident, full of graphs that leaned the same direction as its conclusion. The Cardiff piece was shorter and had the smell of a man who had expected a different answer. What bothered Jayden wasn't the disagreement. It was the suspicion, small at first, that if he kept searching databases he would keep finding Torontos, article after article agreeing with each other, and the Cardiff paper would turn out to be the weird one, the outlier, the study everyone cited in order to disagree with it.

He texted Torin, who was doing the same assignment and had chosen articles about music practice and memory.

how many articles did you find that say practice works

Torin replied with a screenshot of his search results. Fourteen hits, all positive, one of them titled "Further Evidence For." Jayden stared at the word "Further." Further evidence implied earlier evidence, which implied someone had gone looking and someone had published what they'd found. He typed back: did you find any that say it doesn't work. The typing bubble appeared, disappeared, appeared again. "no. why would anyone publish that."

Why indeed. Jayden pulled his laptop closer and typed the question into a search bar in its plainest form: what happens to studies that find nothing. The first useful result mentioned a psychologist, Robert Rosenthal, and a term from 1979, and Jayden read the sentence twice, slowly, the way you reread a text from someone you thought you understood.

He called Torin instead of texting. "It's called the file drawer problem," he said, before Torin could complain about being interrupted. "Rosenthal, 1979. Studies that get null results, they just sit in somebody's drawer. Never published. So the published record looks more positive than the actual evidence." He heard Torin's chair creak on the other end.

"So my fourteen articles," Torin said.

"Could be the ones that made it out of the drawer."

They were quiet for a second, both of them absorbing the size of it. Jayden looked at his two articles again and felt the ground shift under his position, which was the problem, because now he had to build one. He wrote a first line and deleted it. Wrote another. On the table his mother's mail had accumulated, and on top sat a remittance slip from his grandfather, twenty pounds folded inside like it was still 1979 somewhere, and Jayden set it aside without registering it, the way the whole world gets set aside when you're seventeen and the essay is due Monday.

He worked until the window went dark and the highlighter had marked up his hand as much as the pages. The Toronto study was bigger, cleaner, more convincing, and he now distrusted his own sense of what convincing meant, because convincing might just mean lucky, or published, or the survivor. He drafted a paragraph saying the evidence favored a real effect. He drafted a paragraph saying the record was endemic with agreement precisely because disagreement went unpublished, and that the Cardiff study might be rarer than it was wrong. Then he sat with both paragraphs, cursor blinking between them like it was counting something.

His father came through again, printer pages under his arm, and paused at the table. "Still at it?"

"Both of these could be true," Jayden said. "That's the part nobody warns you about." He pulled the page back toward himself and, at the bottom of the second draft, typed: and what remains uncertain is how much we cannot see.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Sabbath commandment appears twice in the Hebrew Bible with different reasons: Exodus 20 cites God resting after creation, while Deuteronomy 5 cites Israel's release from slavery in Egypt.
story:
Kyle spread the two photocopies side by side on the kitchen table, the way Adriel had shown him at lunch, and weighted the curling corners with his mother's mug and a jar of pens. The plan for Saturday's debate round was simple on its face: resolve that the Sabbath commandment, whatever it meant, no longer applied to modern life. Adriel had picked the topic, and Kyle had agreed with the insouciant confidence of someone who had never actually read the texts involved. Now he read them, and the table went quiet except for the furnace ticking in the floor.

The commandment appeared twice in the Hebrew Bible, once in Exodus and once in Deuteronomy, and at first the two versions seemed identical. Keep the day. No work, not for you, not for your household, not for the stranger inside your gates. But when he set his thumb under the reasons attached to each, the sameness broke apart. Exodus 20 grounded the commandment in God resting after creation. Deuteronomy 5 said something else entirely: remember that you were a slave in Egypt, and the Lord brought you out, therefore keep the day. He read both passages again, then a third time, and the third time was the one where the floor of his argument gave way.

His phone buzzed against the wood. Melia, his debate partner, asking if he'd found anything usable for the negative case. He typed that he'd found something better and worse at once, then deleted it and just sent the page numbers.

When his mother came home she stood in the doorway with grocery bags still on her hip and asked what he was doing to her mug. "Debate," he said. "Whether an old religious rule still applies now." She set the bags down and drifted over, and for a moment he thought she would keep walking, but she stopped at the table and read the underlined lines, her lips moving slightly. "Your grandfather kept it," she said, which was not an answer, and also was.

He had been planning to argue that the rule was a relic, that a commandment written for a world of shepherds could not bind people with shift work and exams. But the two different reasons had quietly captivated him, because they pulled in opposite directions. If the day was about creation, then it belonged to everybody, an anthropology rather than a tribal memory. If it was about Egypt, then it was about a specific people who had been freed from a specific bondage, and the commandment read less like ritual and more like a law against exhaustion. Two books. The same commandment. Two rationales. He could argue either one, or he could argue that a rule capable of carrying two reasons was harder to dismiss than a rule with only one.

Melia came over at seven with her laptop and a bag of clementines, and they worked while the kitchen filled with the smell of the onions Kyle's mother had started without being asked. Melia's position was blunt: the class would not care about textual variants, they cared about whether their opponents could defend the resolution. "So we make them defend it," Kyle said. "If the commandment's own book can't agree on why it exists, then which version are they defending?" Melia peeled a clementine in one unbroken spiral, watching him. "That's not a rebuttal," she said. "That's a question." "Questions win rounds," he said, and she conceded the point with a shrug that meant she was thinking about it.

The problem was the veracity of his own conviction. He wanted to believe the argument he was building, and he could feel himself believing it a little too easily, the way you believe anything that wins. He said as much to Melia, who looked at him over the laptop. "Since when do you care?" "Since my mom read the thing over my shoulder like it was a person she knew." Melia was quiet for a moment, which for her was a kind of apology.

Ms. Kang, who lived in the basement apartment and came up some evenings for the mail, arrived at eight with a misdelivered package. Kyle, without quite planning to, asked her whether she thought old rules expired. She considered the question while holding his mother's package of coffee filters like evidence. "Rules don't expire," she said. "People stop needing them, or people start needing them again, and usually you can't tell which until later." Then she took her mail and went back downstairs, leaving the three of them in the kitchen with the onions and the two photocopies and no closing argument at all.

His mother put plates on the table and said he should eat something before he argued with the whole world on an empty stomach. At the table, after Melia had gone, Kyle read the Deuteronomy line aloud, the one about the slave and the release, and asked his mother which reason her father would have said was the real one. She took her time with her fork.

"The one about being tired," she said, and turned off the stove.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In gleaning programs, food bank volunteers harvest crops that remain in farm fields after the main harvest, food that would otherwise go to waste.
story:
Brianna had signed up because the community food bank shared a building with the animal shelter, and her mother had said, wrongly, that she would be walking dogs. Instead she stood on a Saturday morning in a cold side room between stacked crates of dented cans and a wall of kennel noise, while a woman with a clipboard explained sorting procedures and a man behind her weighed bags of squash on a hanging scale.

Maeve had come for the hours, plainly, and said so. "Forty by November," she told Brianna, wiping her hands on her jeans. "The applications want service, and service wants evidence." Naila, who had arrived with a tote bag of her own to fill, wanted something quieter: her family had used a food bank two winters ago, and she never said so directly, only that she knew which shelves ran empty first and that she wanted to be on the other side of the table this time. Brianna, who wanted neither hours nor penance exactly, had a harder time naming her own reason, which was that she had lately begun to feel that opinions were cheap and hands were not.

The problem arrived with the squash. A farmer up the road had called to say his main harvest was done, but the field was still full of fruit the machines and crews had left behind, and the food bank could have it if someone came to get it that morning. The clipboard woman asked for four volunteers. Nobody moved. "It's called gleaning," she said. "You'll be harvesting what's left in the field after the main harvest, food that would otherwise go to waste." Naila raised her hand immediately. Maeve looked at her phone, at the hours log, at the door.

"It doesn't count the same," Maeve said on the drive out in the shelter's ancient van, whose engine sounded frankly moribund and whose heater worked only on the driver's side. "Sorting boxes in a warm room, an hour is an hour. Squash in a cold field, who's tracking that?" Brianna suspected she was half joking, but only half, and she found she could not dismiss it. Maeve's world said a thing mattered when it was counted, recorded, weighed, the way the hanging scale weighed each bag in grams. Naila's world said a thing mattered when someone hungry got it, whether or not anyone wrote it down. Brianna sat between them and held both ideas without dropping either.

The field was brown and stubbled, the farmer a brisk man who pointed at a far row and went back to his truck. The squash lay everywhere the harvesters had passed over: crooked ones, small ones, ones with a soft spot on one cheek, dozens of them, perfectly good on the other side. Naila crouched and began filling a crate with a competence that suggested she had done field work before. Brianna followed her example, and the work was colder and better than the sorting room, her breath fogging, her fingers going stiff around each stem.

"It's a travesty, honestly," Naila said after a while, lifting a fat butternut out of the dirt. "All this, and it would just rot here because it's the wrong shape for a supermarket." Maeve, who had come after all,phone in her pocket, photographing full crates for her log, paused over the word. She was quiet for a moment, then said, "I was going to expatiate on college essays the whole ride, sorry." She picked up two squash at once. "Put me on the record, though. Hours are still hours."

By noon they had filled the van's back row, and the farmer came out to look and gave them each a small misshapen one to keep, the kind he couldn't sell. At the shelter building, the clipboard woman weighed the crates and wrote numbers in her book, and Maeve leaned over to check them, and Naila carried the first crate inside past the kennels, where the dogs were barking at the smell of earth on everyone's shoes.

Brianna still did not know which way of counting was the true one, whether service done for a record was worth less, whether worth could even be measured like that, and she carried her crooked squash out to the van thinking that both things could be so at once. Naila came back for the second crate and bumped her shoulder against Brianna's on the way in. "Take that one home to your mom," she said. "Tell her you did walk dogs."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Near the edges of real plates the field lines bulge outward and the field weakens, an effect called fringing, so E = V/d holds best near the centre.
story:
The physics lab at the science museum occupied a back corner on the second floor, a spartan room of grey tables and cinderblock, wedged between the butterfly hall and the cafeteria's steaming vents. Madeline had chosen it deliberately, or told herself she had, because the placement test for the college physics track was in eleven days and because her bedroom at home had become a place where she could not think about volts at all. Warren had come along out of loyalty and Morgan because Morgan's mother worked the front desk and could get them in free, and now the three of them stood around a demonstration apparatus with two brass plates mounted a hand-span apart, a voltmeter clipped across them, and a small handheld field probe that Ms. Cheung, the lab's supervisor, had checked out to them with the warning not to drop it.

"Twelve hundred volts," Warren read off the meter. "And the gap's, what, six centimetres. So you just divide."

Madeline wrote it out anyway, because writing it out was the whole discipline: E equals V over d, twelve hundred divided by six hundredths of a metre, twenty thousand volts per metre. The formula had a tidiness that she distrusted and wanted at the same time, the way she distrusted anything that promised the world could be reduced to a single clean fraction. She had spent the spring arguing with Morgan about exactly this, late conversations in which Morgan claimed that all of physics was a confidence trick and Madeline claimed that a confidence trick that landed rovers on comets deserved some credit, and those arguments had felt more alive than most of her actual coursework.

The lab station came with a worksheet, and the worksheet's third question had a diagram of the two plates with five marked points: one dead centre, one halfway out, three close to the edges. Madeline was supposed to predict the field at each point and then measure. She predicted twenty thousand volts per metre at all five, drew the same arrow five times, felt the small pleasure of a page that was finished.

Then she measured. At the centre the probe read what the formula said, nearly to the digit, and she felt the specific satisfaction of the universe agreeing with her arithmetic. But at the point near the right edge the reading came up low, not twenty thousand but something stubbornly less, and at the left edge lower still. She recalibrated the probe. She checked the clip leads. She made Warren hold the meter while she steadied the probe with both hands, as though stillness were the missing variable, and the number refused to move upward.

"Your battery's dying," Warren said. "Or your formula's lying."

"It's not lying." But she was no longer sure what to say it was doing. She moved the probe slowly from the centre toward the edge and watched the reading sag as she went, a smooth decay rather than a sudden break, which ruled out a dead battery and a broken probe in one long quiet slide of digits. The field was strong in the middle and weaker near the edges, and the drop-off was gradual, as if the field were leaking sideways out of the gap instead of holding its ranks.

"Try the other edge," Morgan said, leaning in over her shoulder. "If it drops there too, it's not your equipment, it's the plates."

It dropped there too, nearly identically. Madeline stood back with her hands in her pockets and looked at the apparatus as if seeing the category of object for the first time. Somewhere in her memory a lecture hall surfaced, a first-year demonstration she'd watched through a doorway on a campus visit, the professor scattering iron filings between two plates and the filings bulging outward where they neared the ends, curving away like a crowd leaving through the side exits. She hadn't known it had a name. She raised her hand like an idiot and then lowered it, and Ms. Cheung, restocking conductive paper at the supply bench, noticed anyway.

"It's called fringing," Ms. Cheung said, not looking up. "It's in the chapter you haven't got to yet."

"Fringing," Madeline repeated, and wrote the word in the margin of her worksheet beside the two numbers that disagreed. She understood, in a way that arrived without words first, that the formula hadn't lied either; it had simply been answering a narrower question than the one she'd asked. E equals V over d held near the centre, where the field ran straight and uniform, and near the edges of real plates the field lines bulged outward and weakened, and both of those facts were true at once, about the same apparatus, in the same room. It was like the arguments with Morgan: the claim that physics was a trick and the claim that it worked were not opposites but partial answers to different questions, and the honest position was to hold them together and admit where each one thinned out.

She thought of her father, who had wanted her to be a poet, and who had once said that equations would debilitate her imagination the way a corset debilitated a ribcage. She had chosen the equations partly to prove him wrong and partly, she suspected, to wound him a little, and standing here with the probe warm in her palm she could not yet decide whether the choice had been a defection or a discovery. Existentialism had seemed, in the spring, like the only honest response to a world with no guarantees; but the field meter had just told her something no amount of sincerity would have found, and it had also told her something the formula alone would have hidden.

"On the worksheet," Morgan said, tapping the page. "Question three wants your measured values and an explanation. What are you going to write?"

Madeline picked the probe back up and started a fresh column, centre to edge, recording each number in order. "That the formula's right in the middle," she said, "and that I measured at the edge."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: A 2001 review titled 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good', led by Roy Baumeister, found that negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size.
story:
The peer mediation room smelled like the chalk dust of the chemistry lab next door, and Brooklyn sat with her feedback worksheet curled at one corner, the way paper curls when a fist has held it too long. Ms. Anderson had paired them for the exercise: Brooklyn would coach Jadyn through her debate rebuttal, and the whole junior team would watch. Jadyn wanted the varsity slot that opened in January, wanted it so badly she had asked for this public session herself, on the theory that being corrected in front of everyone would prove she could take correction. Brooklyn had agreed before she understood what she was agreeing to.

Jadyn delivered the rebuttal standing, hands moving like she was clearing a table. Her evidence was strong, her transitions quick, and her closing argument, the part she had rewritten four times, collapsed into a rush in which three separate points were jammed into a single breath. Brooklyn knew it immediately, the way you know a stair is missing under your foot.

In September, before any of this, Brooklyn had made a study of how to say things. She had found a review from 2001, led by a researcher named Roy Baumeister, called "Bad Is Stronger Than Good," and it had rearranged something in her. The finding was simple: negative events and remarks usually affected people more strongly than positive ones of a similar size. She had tested it without meaning to. After Laetitia's first tournament speech, Brooklyn had given her five compliments and one criticism, a small criticism, barely a criticism at all, and Laetitia had remembered only that. For two weeks. Brooklyn had watched her friend carry it around like an encumbrance, a weight out of all proportion to its origin, and had not known how to take it back.

"Okay," Ms. Anderson said from the back. "Brooklyn, feedback."

Brooklyn stood. Twelve faces, a clock ticking somewhere above the whiteboard, and Jadyn waiting with her chin lifted in a way that Brooklyn recognized as armor. The old method would have been to lead with the good, bury the bad in a sandwich of praise, hope the praise insulated the blow. But the research had made that strategy feel dishonest, a trick that worked on the giver more than the receiver. At the same time, blurting the flaw first, with no frame around it, seemed guaranteed to make it the only thing Jadyn heard for the rest of the week. Two models of kindness, and they pointed in different directions.

She decided to contextualize instead of cushion. "Your evidence in the second section was the strongest I've heard from anyone on this team," she said, "and I'm saying that first because it's true, not because something bad is coming. Something hard is coming, though, and I want you to hear both things at the same weight, even though I know that's nearly impossible."

Jadyn's arms crossed, then uncrossed, an incipient retreat that she caught halfway.

"In your close, you made three arguments in one sentence, and the third one, the one about precedent, got lost. I think it might be your best point. It came out so fast that nobody in the round could have caught it." Brooklyn made herself stay specific: which sentence, which argument, what was lost, why it mattered. Not "you rushed." Not "the ending was weak." The flaw, named precisely, and attached to something Jadyn herself valued.

Jadyn was quiet for a moment, and Brooklyn felt the old fear rise, the fear that she had wounded her friend in front of witnesses and that the wound would outlast everything else said in this room. But Jadyn pulled the speech off the desk and turned to the last page, running her pen under the tangled sentence. "The precedent one," she said. "That's the one I stayed up for." She looked at Brooklyn, and something in her face was working, not gratitude exactly, but calculation, the recalculation of a person deciding what to keep. "Say the first part again. The part about the evidence."

"Strongest on the team."

"Both at the same weight," Jadyn repeated, mostly to herself, and marked the page.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Decision in US college admissions is binding: a student admitted with acceptable financial aid must enroll and withdraw all other applications.
story:
The letter had come as an email, which felt like a cheat, and Sierra had printed it at the library because some things deserved paper. She read it a fourth time at the corner table of the coffee shop, the paper soft at the folds already, the smell of burnt espresso settling over everything. Sonya slid into the opposite chair with two hot chocolates and put one in front of her like an offering meant to assuage whatever was on the page.

"Read it out loud," Sonya said.

"You can't apply Early Decision to a school and then shop around," Sierra said. "It's binding. If they let you in and the financial aid is acceptable, you have to go, and you have to pull every other application." She flattened the page against the table. "I didn't get that before November. I mean, I got it in a words way, but I didn't get it."

"You got into Ellsworth," Sonya said. "That's the headline, Sierra."

"The headline is that I never found out what money anywhere else would have offered me." She said it without raising her voice, then looked at the window, where a man was taping a cardboard snowflake crooked to the glass. Sonya drank her chocolate and waited, the way she'd learned to wait in eleven years of friendship.

The truth was uglier and older than the email. In October, Sierra had wanted Ellsworth so badly that she'd made herself impermeable to argument, nodding through Sonya's questions about aid, smiling past her mother's face at the kitchen table when she said she'd handle the forms. At the time it had felt like conviction. Now it felt like something closer to fear wearing conviction's coat. The counselor had slid the Early Decision agreement across the desk and Sierra had signed it in her neatest handwriting, as if neatness were a kind of insurance.

Luke came in shaking rain off his jacket and read the letter upside down from the counter, which he could do, one of his useless talents. "So it's over," he said, sitting down. "You're going. That's the dream, isn't it?"

"That depends on what the aid package looks like," Sierra said. "If it's acceptable. That's the word they use. If it isn't, I'm not bound, but then it's basically December again with no applications anywhere else, since I had to withdraw them all." She heard herself laying the logic out flat and clinical, a way of keeping her hands from shaking. "My mom makes it sound like a bargain either way. Mr. Popal makes it sound like a trap."

Mr. Popal taught physics two doors down from the college counselor and bought his coffee here every afternoon at three, regular in a chipped blue mug, which the owner kept for him on a shelf above the beans. When he came in, Sierra raised the letter half an inch. He carried his mug over, stood at the end of their table, and said only, "The body likes homeostasis, but it's not the body's job to stay comfortable. It's the body's job to stay alive." Then he went to his usual stool and opened his crossword, and Sierra understood that the comment was the whole conversation, and that it belonged to her, not to the college.

She took out her phone and drafted a message to her mother, thumbed it, deleted it, drafted again. When she finally sent it, the screen read: I want us to sit with the aid letter tonight before I say yes out loud. I know I have to say yes if it's okay money. But I want us to look at okay together. That's all. Below the message she typed a second one to herself, in the notes app, a habit she'd stolen from Sonya: What I believe now is that loving a school first and asking questions second got the order backwards. What I don't know yet is whether backwards is still where I end up. She locked the phone and set it face down.

She folded the printed letter once, twice, until it fit in her jacket's inner pocket, the one closest to her chest. The cardboard snowflake outside had come unstuck and hung from one piece of tape, turning in the draft from the door. Sierra picked up the hot chocolate Sonya had brought her, still warm, and drank.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note one octave higher than another vibrates at exactly twice its frequency, so the A above A440 is 880 hertz.
story:
Hayden had signed out the cello three weeks ago with a requisition form so prolix it required both a teacher's signature and a parent's, as though the school were entrusting him with something more dangerous than a plywood instrument with a crack running down its back. He had wanted the cello because his grandmother played one, or had played one, before her hands stiffened and the instrument went to a cousin in another province. He could not have explained the wanting beyond that.

The music room smelled of valve oil and radiator dust. Mondays after last bell, Mr. Eze left the door unlocked for the students who practiced on their own, and Hayden took the corner by the window where the music stands kept their crooked habit of leaning. Sharon was already there, tuning her violin against the grey box tuner clipped to her stand, and Mylee sat on the radiator cover with her phone, supposedly listening, probably not.

He had been stuck on the A string for a week. His first finger kept landing flat, and the tuner's needle swung left of centre like something refusing to be convinced. Sharon watched him struggle for a while, then came over, took the bow out of his hand, and played his open string for him. The needle steadied. She pointed at the little screen. "Four forty," she said. "That's what an A is, on the tuner. Four forty."

Hayden had not thought of a note as a number before. He played the open A again himself, watching the needle settle at 440, and then, because he was sixteen and suspicious of anything that came too easily, he slid his hand up the string and put his fourth finger down where the higher A lived. Or where he thought it lived. The needle lurched right, nearly off the dial, and the number came up wrong. Not a little wrong. Eight eighty.

He stared at it. He had expected the number to be higher, obviously, but not like this. He played the low A, then the high one, then both again while Mylee, despite herself, leaned in over his shoulder. "It doubled," she said. "Exactly double. That's kind of gross." She meant it as a compliment to the universe.

He wrote it on the back of his practice sheet: A is 440, the A above it is 880, one octave up means twice the frequency. Nothing on the sheet told him why, and he found he liked that. In physics last term, Mr. Eze, who apparently taught across the hall some years, had once said that metonymy was when you call a thing by something associated with it, like calling the violin section "the strings," and Hayden had a sudden foolish sense that the number 440 was like that too. It wasn't the note. It was a name the note went by in the tuner's language.

His grandmother would have known this already. Or maybe not. He thought of the summer he was nine, sitting on her kitchen floor while she played scales with her eyes closed, and how he had asked her once why the notes repeated, why there was an A and then another A higher up, like a stairway that came back around. She had said something about the circle of it, how the same note came back thinner and brighter, and he had accepted that the way children accept weather. Now the tuner told him it was plainer than a circle. It was the same thing, doubled.

Except it wasn't the same thing, and this was where he got stuck, that Monday and the Monday after. The high A felt different under his finger. It sang where the low one hummed. If it were really just the same note doubled, then why did his chest do something different when Sharon played it up there in a melody? He tried the question out on Mylee, who shrugged and said that doubling water didn't make it a different drink. Sharon said that was the worst analogy she had ever heard, and they argued about it through the whole of Hayden's practice time, which he did not mind.

He thought about the choice he had made in September, too, when Mr. Eze had offered him trumpet instead. Easier, Mr. Eze had said, easier to sound good on, faster to place you in the ensemble. Hayden had said no without knowing why, and he still didn't know whether the no had been stubbornness or something better. Maybe the cello was a mistake. Maybe the mistake was the point. He held both ideas the way he held the bow now, with a grip his teacher would still call too tight.

In the last ten minutes of the room's open hour, he tried an experiment. He played the low A and asked Sharon to play the high one at the same time, on her violin, tuned to her own little grey box. The two notes landed together and something happened in the air between them, a shimmer, like the sound agreeing with itself. Mylee stopped looking at her phone. Neither of them said anything for a second.

"Do it again," Sharon said, already lifting her bow.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together.
story:
Elijah sat on the floor of his half-empty bedroom, surrounded by boxes labeled in his mother's tidy hand, holding a shoebox of receipts and ticket stubs he had no intention of throwing out. The movers came on Thursday. Two days from now, and everything he owned would be reassembled in a town four hours north, where nobody knew that he always ordered the same wrong thing at the noodle place and then traded half of it away. He sorted the stubs into piles: movie with Alexis, movie with Freya, the tragic evening both of them came and argued about whose turn it was to pick.

Alexis arrived at three, as promised, carrying a bag of oranges because she claimed that peeling them kept her from saying stupid things. She sat cross-legged on the mattress, which was already stripped, and pointed at the shoebox. "Is that your museum?"

"It's the archive," Elijah said. "Every ticket from every movie since tenth grade."

"You kept the one from the film we walked out of?"

"Especially that one." He held it up. The print had faded to a ghost of itself, but he could still read the date. Something about the stub made him wonder, and he said so out loud, because Alexis tolerated that in him. "How many hours do you think are in this box? Like, if you added them all up."

"Together? With me?" She peeled an orange in one long unbroken spiral, which was showing off. "I mean, we've known each other since we were eleven. That's a lot of movies, a lot of bus rides, a lot of you being late."

Freya let herself in through the back door, the way she always had, and stood in the doorway holding her phone. She had a way of looking nonchalant that never quite worked; the phone was upside down in her hand. "Okay, so I fell down a rabbit hole last night, because I was trying to figure out how long it takes to make a friend. Like from scratch. At the new school." She paused. "For you. Obviously for you."

"And?" Elijah said.

"There's this study. Some researcher, Hall, 2018. He estimated it. Becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together." She scrolled as though checking her own memory against the screen. "Two hundred. More than that."

The room went quiet except for the sound of Alexis snapping a segment of orange in half. Elijah did the arithmetic before he could stop himself, which was a habit his mother called charming and his father called incurable. "We've been at school together, what, six hours a day, a hundred and eighty days a year, for four years," he said slowly. "Even if you only count a fraction of that as actual together time."

"Stop," Alexis said. "You're going to tell me we're rich."

"We're millionaires." He laughed, and then, because the laugh had somewhere to fall, it fell. He looked at the shoebox. Two hundred hours. It wasn't the number that got him, it was the shape of it: friendship as something accumulated, hour by hour, like sediment. He had always thought of his friendships as fixed, as things you either had or didn't, and now here was evidence that they were built, which meant they could also be unbuilt, or left half-built in a town four hours south.

"That's the sad version," Freya said, watching his face. "There's another version, though. If it's hours, then it's doable. It's not luck or chemistry or whatever bromide people say about friendship. You just show up. A lot. Over and over."

"That sounds terrible," Alexis said. "Showing up on purpose. Like a job."

"Would you demur," Freya said, "if the job had good coworkers?"

Elijah turned a ticket stub over in his fingers. He liked both versions and could not make them into one. The hours in the box were real, and he was leaving them, and that loss was not a metaphor; it was Thursday, a truck, four hours of highway. But Freya's version was also real: whatever waited in the new town would have to be assembled the same slow way, which meant it could be assembled, which meant the leaving was not an ending so much as the start of somebody else's shoebox. He didn't say any of this. He held up the stub from the movie they'd walked out of.

"I want you to have this," he told Alexis.

"We hated that movie."

"That's why. It's proof we left."

Alexis took it, considered it, and tucked it into the pocket of her jacket, over her heart, which ruined the effect by making her laugh. Freya, who had been quiet for a moment, cleared her throat and said, "So when you get there, find somebody with a free block after lunch." She tapped the shoebox. "You have two hundred hours to bank. Better start the deposit."

Elijah put the lid on the box, stood, and carried it to the pile marked for the truck, placing it on top where it would ride in plain sight the whole way north.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Children accounted for about one-third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, according to Food Banks Canada's HungerCount report.
story:
Ms. Bakker handed Robert a hairnet as though it were a diploma. "Ladle line," she said. "You're with Lukas."

The kitchen smelled of onions and floor cleaner, and behind the serving window a line had already formed, longer than Robert had expected for a Saturday. Lukas worked the tray slide with the ease of someone who had done this many Saturdays, sliding bowls, adding bread, saying "morning" to each person in a voice that somehow made it a real question. Robert's job was rice, and for the first ten minutes he mostly watched Lukas and spilled nothing, which he counted as an achievement.

Josh arrived late, wearing the same shirt from the school assembly where their guidance counsellor had pitched volunteer hours as "a chance to build character," a phrase Josh had found gratuitous at the time and found more so now. He was assigned to the storeroom to pack hampers for the family program, and he kept drifting back to the ladle line to report his findings. "Every hamper has crackers in it," he said. "Also baby cereal. I've packed, like, forty, and the baby cereal is constant. It's the sun around which everything else orbits."

"You should be doing inventory, not astronomy," Lukas said.

"I'm doing both. I contain multitudes."

It was on the notice board by the storeroom door, between a hand-washing diagram and a sign-up sheet, that Robert found the number. Josh had flattened a flyer to use as a coaster, and beneath the coffee ring the print was still legible: children accounted for about one-third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, according to Food Banks Canada's HungerCount report. He read it twice, then stood there holding the flyer with a strange reluctance to put it down, as if the paper itself were a tray he might spill.

He tried to think about it while he ladled. At school the calculus was different: hunger was an abstraction, something in photographs, something a person did a sponsored run against. Here it had crackers and baby cereal and constant, orbiting regularity. He could not manage to hold both pictures at once. When he tried to verbalize any of it to Lukas between trays, what came out was "A third of the visits were kids. In March. Like, one in three." Lukas nodded without stopping the slide. "That's the flyer on the board," he said. "I read it my first week. You get used to the number. I don't know if that's good or bad."

The line thinned toward one o'clock, and the attrition of volunteers began: Josh vanished to find the washroom and did not return for twenty minutes; a woman from the church group left early, mentioning a rehearsal. Robert stayed on rice until the pot was scraped thin. A boy about ten came through with a woman who might have been his grandmother, and Robert gave him an extra spoonful, then worried that the extra spoonful was a kind of insult, then worried that worrying about it was worse. The boy said thank you. He had a loose tooth and said it around.

Ms. Bakker asked him, at the end, whether he would be back. He understood that this was the moment to say something conclusive, that she likely heard speeches from teenagers all the time about perspective and gratitude. "I don't know yet," he said. "The number. A third of visits being kids. It's not what I thought the number would be. I'm not sure what I thought it would be."

"That's an honest answer," she said. "Most people give me a speech."

On the walk to the bus stop, Josh was still holding the last hamper list, folded into his pocket, and Robert realized he was still holding the flyer, coffee ring and all. Josh asked what he was going to do with it. Robert looked at it for a moment, then at the bus turning the corner, and said, "I'm going to put it on my wall and see what happens."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Guessing a whole number from 1 to 100 by always picking the middle of the remaining range never takes more than seven guesses, which is binary search in game form.
story:
Ashley sat at the kitchen table with her laptop open to an empty file named search_stuff_v3, which was optimistic, since versions one and two had produced nothing but error messages. The assignment from Ms. Yilmaz was due Monday: implement a search on a sorted list and explain why one approach beat another. Ashley understood the words individually. Arranged in that order, they defeated her.

Her grandfather, recuperating on the couch from a knee operation the whole family referred to as "the knee," had been watching her stare at the screen for twenty minutes. "When I was your age," he said, "we didn't have homework that could stare back. Want to play a game? I'm bored and you're not getting anywhere."

"One game," Ashley said, because it was true, she wasn't getting anywhere.

"Pick a whole number from one to a hundred. Don't tell me. I'll guess it and you say higher or lower."

She chose sixty-three and felt a small, mean pleasure, because sixty-three was neither round nor obvious. Her grandfather put on his glasses with great ceremony, as though gravitas might improve his odds. "Fifty," he said.

"Higher."

"Seventy-five."

"Lower." She waited for him to flounder the way her little cousin did, wandering up and down the numbers one at a time like someone hunting for a dropped earring.

"Sixty-two."

"Higher," she said, sitting up a little.

"Sixty-three?"

"Yes. Okay, luck."

"Again," he said. "New number."

She chose nine. He said fifty, then twenty-five, then twelve, then six, then nine. Five guesses. She chose a hundred and he reached it in seven: fifty, seventy-five, eighty-eight, ninety-four, ninety-seven, ninety-nine, a hundred. Seven again. Something in her head tilted sideways. "Wait," she said. "Are you doing something?"

"I always pick the middle of what's left," he said. "Guessing a whole number from one to a hundred that way never takes more than seven guesses."

"That's not a game, that's a machine," Ashley said, and then, because she was sixteen and incapable of leaving a wound unexamined, "how long have you known that?"

"Since before your father was born. It's called binary search." He resettled his knee against the cushion, deeply pleased with himself.

Ashley pulled her laptop closer and played it back in her mind, the range cutting in half, then in half again, one hundred numbers collapsing to fifty, to twenty-five, and on down until a single number stood alone in the wreckage. The empty file did not look empty anymore; it looked like it was waiting for the shape she now had. She wrote a loop that kept track of a low and a high, found the middle, and asked the list the same dumb question her grandfather had asked: higher, or lower? When she ran it against a sorted list of a thousand names, it found hers in ten steps. When she swapped in the version that checked every entry from the front, the one she'd written first out of pure habit, it took six hundred and forty. She sat back and heard herself laugh, one short syllable, alone in the kitchen.

That evening she called Sloane, partly to study and mostly to perform. "Okay, think of a number, one to a hundred, I'll get it in seven."

"You'll get seven what?"

"Guesses. Maximum. Pick."

Sloane picked, and Ashley halved her way to it in five, narrating each cut, and Sloane's voice climbed an octave on the last one. Ashley explained the assignment the way she finally understood it: the guessing game was the idea wearing a costume; the code was the same idea in its work clothes. The catch, the part she kept turning over, was that the whole trick only held if the data was sorted, which meant the speed wasn't free, it was paid for somewhere upstream by somebody doing the sorting. She said this out loud to Sloane and then said, "I don't know if I can explain that part yet without it turning into a paragraph Ms. Yilmaz crosses out."

"Say it like you said it to me just now," Sloane said. "Then stop talking."

Monday morning Ashley turned it in, walked home, and found her grandfather at the kitchen table with a deck of cards, shuffling with an expression she recognized from the couch. "New game," he said. "I pick a card, you tell me higher or lower."

"You already won that game," Ashley said. "You invented that game."

"Not with cards," he said, fanning the deck out across the table, every card face up and in no order at all. "It's shuffled."

Ashley looked at the sixty-two scattered cards, none of them in the middle of anything, and reached for the one thing she knew how to do. "First," she said, "we sort them."

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Herman and Chomsky's second filter is advertising: outlets that depend on advertisers' money have a reason to avoid coverage that drives those advertisers away.
story:
The cushions of the couch had gone flat in the middle, and Charles kept sliding toward the low spot while Siena sat cross-legged on the rug with the disputed article spread in front of her. The story itself was short: a used car dealership on Route 9 had sold three students cars with rolled-back odometers, and Siena had documented it with inspection records, photographs of the dashboards, and interviews with two of the buyers. The phone call had come that afternoon, to the adviser's office, and Mr. Tehrani had relayed it to them in his careful, unhurried way: the dealership's owner wanted the article killed, or he would take his advertising elsewhere.

"He pays for a full page every month," Charles said. He was holding the budget they had sketched on the back of a chemistry worksheet. "That's most of what keeps us printing."

Siena did not look up. "So we run it and we print on thinner paper."

He wanted to argue, and the wanting itself bothered him, because he admired her and knew she was right about the cars. He got up and paced the length of the living room, past the shelf where his father kept the good speakers nobody was allowed to touch, and stopped at the window. On the coffee table lay his media studies folder, which he had brought home for the same reason he brought everything home, which was that the apartment was quieter than the library after five. The folder had fallen open to a page of notes from last week's reading, Herman and Chomsky's five filters.

"The second filter is advertising," he read aloud. "Outlets that depend on advertisers' money have a reason to avoid coverage that drives those advertisers away." He said it twice, the second time slower, because the sentence had stopped sounding like homework and started sounding like Tuesday.

Siena finally looked up. "Meaning us."

"Meaning everybody like us." He carried the folder back to the couch and sat on the firm cushion at the end, out of the low spot. The idea was not complicated, and that was what made it heavy. It was not that anyone had ordered them to lie. It was that the money had opinions before anyone opened their mouth, and the dealership owner did not even have to make the call he had made, because papers all over the country absorbed that lesson quietly, every day, without a threat arriving first. He thought of the campus paper his sister used to read, how its restaurant reviews were mysteriously gentle, and he could no longer tell whether that had been politeness or arithmetic.

"We could run the story with his ads," Siena said. "Take his money this month and print the truth about him in the same issue."

"That's worse. That's using him."

"It's him using us either way." She stretched out a leg and knocked his ankle with her foot, not quite gently. "You want there to be a clean option. There isn't one."

Mr. Tehrani had said something similar, in his way, though he had framed it as a question, the way he framed everything, as if the answer were a word Charles should be able to pronounce if he slowed down enough. Charles thought of the phonetics unit he had half-finished in another class, the way a word could look unmanageable on the page and turn out to be simple once you broke it into sounds. He felt the same thing happening here. Kill the story: cowardly. Run it and lose the funding: principled and possibly fatal to the paper. Run it beside the ads: shrewd and a little dirty. Each option sat in his mouth differently.

He took out his phone and called Mr. Tehrani, who answered on the second ring and listened while Charles laid out the three options in order, without recommending any of them. There was a pause on the line, and then a sound like a chair creaking.

"There's a fourth option," Mr. Tehrani said. "The alumni association asked me last spring whether the paper needed anything. I told them no because we had the dealership. You could ask them now, before the next issue. You would still have to decide what to do if they say no."

Charles repeated it to Siena, holding the phone against his shoulder. She was already pulling the article toward her, smoothing the crease where she had folded it in anger an hour ago.

"We run it," she said. "Whatever the money does. Even if we end up as some parochial little sheet printed off the library copier." She looked at the two students in the photographs, their hands on the hoods of cars that had lied to them. "Call the alumni people tonight. I'll stay and finish the layout."

Charles dialed, and while the phone rang he watched her begin, in silence, to mark the places where the column would break.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The shelf label's unit price shows the cost per gram, litre or item, which lets shoppers compare packages of different sizes fairly.
story:
The binder had been his grandmother's, and it still smelled faintly of pencil shavings and the lemon cleaner she wiped the kitchen table with on Sundays. Jack sat at that table now, the house too quiet since her hip surgery, and copied her old system onto fresh paper: seven dinners, one shopping list, quantities in the margins. She had planned meals this way for fifty years, he remembered, announcing Saturday's soup on Monday as though the future were a guest already expected. The doctor had said she'd need weeks of recovery, and his mother had said, half a question, that maybe Jack could handle the food for a while. He had said yes before he understood what yes contained.

The list took him three evenings. He read about cooking in batches, about soaking beans overnight, about roasting two trays of vegetables when the oven was already hot. It felt like a kind of engineering, and he liked that, liked imagining the week as a structure that would hold. He called his friend Anita, who had worked a summer at a bakery and knew what "mise en place" meant, and she talked him out of a recipe that required four kinds of vinegar. His classmate Leonidas, who lived two streets over, offered to come shopping because his uncle managed the store and Leonidas claimed insider knowledge of the aisles. Jack agreed mostly for the company.

The store on Saturday afternoon was bright and loud, refrigerators humming like a held breath. Jack worked down his list with a pencil, crossing items off, and at the cereal aisle he picked up a large bag of rolled oats, nearly double the size of the small one. He was reaching for it when he hesitated and looked at the shelf label instead of the price. Beneath the big bold number there was a smaller figure, and he read it twice.

"It's the unit price," he said, tapping the label. "The shelf label's unit price shows the cost per gram, litre or item, so you can compare packages of different sizes fairly."

Leonidas leaned in, skeptical. "My uncle says the big bags are always the deal."

"Then your uncle would lose money on this one." Jack held up both bags. The larger bag's unit price, per gram, was higher than the small one's. He did the arithmetic in his notebook margin to be sure, because it destabilized something he'd believed without ever having examined it, the same way he'd always assumed his grandmother bought whatever was largest. Maybe she had known. Maybe she'd just had more mouths to feed.

They filled the cart slowly, checking labels, arguing gently about whether the store brand of crushed tomatoes was worth the savings. Anita texted him a reminder about eggs and a joke about his "rectitude," because he had refused to buy cookies not on the list, and he typed back that the list was a moral document, which was only half a joke. At the checkout he watched the total climb past what he'd estimated and felt the week's structure flex. He paid from the envelope his mother had left, counted the change twice, and carried the bags home with Leonidas carrying two, both of them quiet in the way of boys doing something new and not wanting to name it.

Sunday he cooked. The kitchen filled with steam and the smell of onions he had cut badly, eyes streaming, and Ms. Reyes from next door knocked on the screen door to say the exhaust fan was supposed to be on, and stayed to show him how the auxiliary burner on the old stove ran hotter than the others. She told a story about his grandmother burning rice every anniversary for a decade before giving up and making pasta instead, and Jack laughed and ladled soup into containers for Tuesday and Thursday, labeled them, and stacked them in the freezer like files. His grandmother called from the rehab center during the afternoon and asked what he'd bought. He told her about the oats, the two bags, the shelf labels. There was a pause on the line long enough that he thought the call had dropped.

"I never looked at those," she said.

"You had four kids. You were just trying to get through the aisle."

"I was," she said, and then, softer, "I was." He didn't know whether to feel proud or sad, so he told her about the soup instead, and the beans he'd forgotten to soak until eleven at night, and she laughed at that, really laughed, and told him to put them in the morning's water before he went to bed, which he did, standing alone in her kitchen after dark, dropping them one at a time into the bowl and listening to each small, definite click.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence.
story:
Rachel had never lost her place in anything, so she was sure the article was still in her hand when she reached the booth at the far end of the festival grounds. It was not. She found it two stalls later, folded into her back pocket along with the map of the food vendors, which she had also not lost, only misplaced. She smoothed the paper on the counter of the newspaper stand and read the first line again, slowly, the way Ms. Chanthavong had taught her, consonant by consonant.

The stand sold Lao newspapers, mostly to the older attendees, and Ms. Chanthavong had agreed to let Rachel attempt her first spoken summary there at four o'clock. Rachel had chosen a short piece about flooding, maybe twelve sentences, and had spent the whole bus ride to the park translating it. She did not get nervous about these things. Dale got nervous, and Ella got nervous, and Rachel watched them do it, the way they fanned themselves with their programs and laughed too loudly at nothing. She simply prepared.

"You're early," Ms. Chanthavong said. She was stacking copies and did not look up. "Four o'clock. You have twenty minutes."

"I like to be early," Rachel said, which was true, and which she felt proved something about her, though she could not have said what.

Ella arrived at ten to four with skewered chicken and stood at Rachel's elbow to listen. Dale trailed behind her with a bottle of orange soda, already bored. Rachel arranged the article on the counter and looked at it one last time. The ink had smudged where her thumb had held the fold, blurring the topmost line into a grey smear, but she had read that line on the bus and she remembered it fine. It was about the river, and how fast it had risen, and how many families had moved their animals.

"It's not a performance," Ms. Chanthavong said, watching her. "You summarize, I listen, I correct. That's all."

"I know," Rachel said. She began.

She read aloud the second sentence, then the third, and then set the paper down and gave the summary in Lao, halting but complete. The river had risen. Families had moved their animals. Roads were closed in the north of the country. She had practiced that last part on the bus, the word for north, and she delivered it with the small satisfaction of a locked door clicking shut.

"Thailand," Ms. Chanthavong repeated. "You said Thailand."

"Yes. The north of Thailand." Rachel was certain. The article had said so, or something near it, and she did not argue because she was not the arguing kind, she simply stated what was in front of her. "The north."

Ms. Chanthavong picked up the paper and held it out. "Read the very top. Before the first sentence."

"The first part's smudged," Rachel said. It was, partly, and the rest she had skipped on the bus because it was short and looked like a heading, and headings were furniture. She had decided that on the bus, at some point, without quite deciding it. Now she squinted at the unsmudged half and sounded it out. It was not part of the flood sentence.
