It was a word she knew from the geography unit, and then a word she knew from the restaurant stall at the end of the row, the one with the papaya salad and the long queue. A city. A city in Laos.

"That's the dateline," Ella said, leaning in, mouth full. "It says where the story was reported. It goes before the first sentence. It's in everything, the papers at home do it too." Dale, behind her, said "huh" in a tone that suggested he had never once read to the top of anything in his life.

Rachel metabolized this the way she metabolized most corrections, which was to say she felt it land somewhere under the ribs and then pretended she had scheduled it herself. "So the story's from Laos," she said. "Vientiane. And the roads are in the north of Laos." She looked at the smudge, and at the clear letters beside it, and at the sentence below, which she had taken as the beginning and which had never been the beginning at all. It was not that she had been careless. She had been efficient, and efficiency had carried her confidently past the one thing that told her where she was.

"The summary is good otherwise," Ms. Chanthavong said. "The grammar is good. Do it again, from the city."

Rachel picked the paper up. Ella wiped her hands on her jeans and settled in for another round. Dale drank his soda. Somewhere behind the stall a drum started up for the five o'clock performance, and Rachel began again, at the top this time, with the name of the city.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: The phrase 'There ain't no such thing as a free lunch' was popularized by its use in Robert Heinlein's 1966 novel The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress.
story:
The gelato stand sat between a shoe store and a cell phone kiosk, close enough to the food court entrance that Joseph could hear the announcer from the promotions booth all afternoon. The booth had a spinning wheel and a table stacked with small canvas tote bags, and every hour or so a voice declared that anyone who completed a short survey would receive a free gift, no purchase necessary. Joseph had worked at the stand for six weeks, long enough to know that the free gift was the same tote bag every time, and that the survey took eleven minutes if you answered slowly and seven if you didn't care.

He wanted the Saturday shift at the smoothie place across the court. It paid two dollars more an hour and the manager let staff take home whatever fruit was too soft to sell. The trouble was that the gelato stand had promoted him to the auxiliary closing position, which meant he counted the till alone on Thursdays and Fridays, and the smoothie place needed him exactly then. Mr. Patel, who owned the gelato stand and half of the dry cleaner two doors down, had already told him the choice was his to make, which was either generous or a way of saying he wouldn't fight to keep him.

Eloise came by on her break from the bookstore, carrying a smoothie she'd bought at half price with a coupon she'd found online. "You should do the survey," she said, nodding toward the booth. "Free bag. You could put your aprons in it."

"There's a catch," Joseph said. He wiped down the counter, though it was already clean. "Nine minutes of questions about where I buy shoes, in exchange for a bag that costs them maybe a dollar. My time is worth more than a dollar." He wasn't sure that was entirely true. He earned minimum wage, which worked out to slightly less than a dollar every six minutes, and the survey would be during his paid break either way.

Kali, who worked the register beside him, had opinions about everything at the food court, including the announcer. "My cousin says that whole booth exists to collect email addresses," she said. "They sell them. So the bag isn't the real product. We're the real product." She said it with the satisfaction of someone who had recently learned the phrase and was still enjoying its shape.

That afternoon a man in a green windbreaker stood at the booth, refusing the clipboard the survey girl offered him. "There ain't no such thing as a free lunch," he said, pleasantly enough, and walked on toward the escalators. Joseph heard it while scooping stracciatella for a customer, and the phrase stayed with him through the dinner rush, partly because it sounded like something his grandfather would have said.

He looked it up on his phone during closing, sitting on the milk crate behind the freezer while the floor dried. He had assumed the saying was ancient, the kind of thing that belonged to no one, like "a stitch in time." Instead the search told him it was popularized by its use in Robert Heinlein's 1966 novel The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress. He read that line twice. A science fiction writer had put the words into circulation, and now a man in a green windbreaker quoted it to a survey girl in a mall as though it had fallen from the sky. In his history class they had just started a unit on historiography, on how versions of the past get built and passed along, and Mr. Dunmore kept saying that tracing an idea to its source changed what you could claim about it. Joseph hadn't believed him, exactly. It was easier to believe it now, holding a phone that said the free lunch was Heinlein's lunch.

The idea was simple enough to be annoying. If he took the smoothie job, the extra two dollars an hour wasn't all he gained; the cost was closing the till alone, the keys on the lanyard, the fact that Mr. Patel had chosen him for it. If he stayed, the cost was the fruit and the money and whatever the smoothie manager might have taught him. Nothing was simply added. Everything was traded.

On Thursday Mr. Patel stopped by while Joseph was reconciling the till. "You've been quiet this week," Mr. Patel said. "Quiet is fine. Brooding is different."

"I'm deciding something."

"The smoothie place." Mr. Patel said it without heat, the way he named flavors, and Joseph felt obscurely exonerated, as though being found out had cleared him of something. "Take it if it's better. Take this if it's better. Only remember that better is a word with more than one meaning, and most people use just the one."

Joseph finished the count, sealed the deposit bag, and hung the lanyard on its hook. The promotions booth was shuttered for the night, its wheel covered in a plastic bag, the stack of totes squared and untouched beneath the fluorescent lights. He thought about the man in the windbreaker, and about Heinlein, and about the survey girl who had probably gone home. On Saturday he walked past the smoothie place, slowed down at the door, and kept walking, all the way to the bookstore, where he asked Eloise if she still had that coupon.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The SAT switched to a digital, adaptive format in the United States in March 2024: how well a student does on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second.
story:
The guidance counselor's office smelled like the inside of a laminator, and Grace had been sitting in the vinyl chair for eleven minutes before Mr. Van Dijk looked up from his screen. On the wall behind him hung a poster that said OPTIONS in a font she suspected had not changed since the building was built, a poster so committed to its own message that it had begun to ossify into wallpaper. "You wanted to talk about early decision," he said, which was not a question, and Grace said yes, and unzipped her backpack, and took out the folder she had organized three times since breakfast.

The folder contained her transcript, her essay draft, and the score report she had checked eleven times in the past week, always hoping the numbers had somehow revised themselves upward out of shame. "The thing is," she said, "I don't know if the score is me." Mr. Van Dijk rotated his monitor so she could see the form she needed, and slid a pen across the desk, and waited in the way of a man who had learned that waiting was most of the job.

She thought about the morning of the test. The room had been cold, the kind of cold that makes your knuckles look foreign, and the proctor had said almost nothing except "begin" and "stop." The math section had opened easily, questions she could have done in her sleep, and she had begun to relax, and then the second half had arrived like a door opening onto weather from another planet. Question after question she didn't recognize. She had spent four minutes on a single problem and felt the whole future narrow to the width of a pencil.

Afterward, in the parking lot, she had told Sylvia it was over, that she had failed, that second module had been igneous, molten, impossible. Sylvia had been unbuttoning her coat and had not stopped unbuttoning it. "It's adaptive," she said. "The SAT's digital now, since March. How you do on the first module of each section sets how hard the second one is." Grace had stood there with her hands in her pockets. "So mine was hard," Sylvia went on, "hard probably means your first one went well." Grace had wanted to argue with this, because wanting to argue was easier than hoping, but Sylvia had only shrugged and said the despot of that exam was a computer somewhere, not a person, and computers at least had rules.

Now, in the office, Grace filled out the top of the form and stopped at the line asking which score report to send. Because there was a choice. She had two of them now: the March one, the adaptive one, the one whose difficulty she could not see from the outside, and an earlier one from a paper year, lower, but legible, a number whose meaning she felt she understood. Her mother preferred the legible number, or preferred any number, because her mother believed that luck was a story people told to avoid accountability. Sylvia believed the opposite, that the whole apparatus was luck wearing a lab coat. Grace had spent two weeks shuttling between them like a courier who was also the package.

"The early deadline's the first of the month," Mr. Van Dijk said. "You can wait for regular decision if the certainty matters." He said it neutrally, the way a man says things neutrally when he has said them four hundred times. Grace looked at the line. The truth was she did not know whether the March score was better or worse than it felt; the difficulty had been invisible to her, the mechanism sealed, and any story she told about it was a story. But Sylvia's explanation was not nothing. It was a rule, stated plainly, and it had survived every attempt Grace had made to disprove it at two in the morning.

"I'll send the March one," she said. "I can't prove it's my best work. But I can't prove it isn't, and the other one I already know isn't." Mr. Van Dijk nodded and turned the monitor back toward himself. "That's a position," he said, which seemed to be his version of praise. Grace signed her name, and the pen skipped once on the laminated surface of the desk, and she signed over the skip.

Outside, the hallway was emptying toward fourth period. She texted Sylvia: sent it. Then, after a moment, she took the poster-worthy folder, squared its edges against the thigh of her jeans, and dropped it neatly into the recycling bin outside the office door, where it landed on top of somebody's discarded course catalog and did not fit.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Two parallel plates 0.02 metres apart with 100 volts across them produce an electric field of 5,000 volts per metre between them.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of hot glue and printer toner, and Connor had spent forty minutes watching judges drift past his table like planets that had not yet decided whether his project exerted any gravity. His display read, in letters he now considered too large, "Electric Fields Between Parallel Plates." Behind him, Calista was arranging and rearranging her seedlings under a grow light, a project on diurnal growth cycles in cress, which she claimed was going to win the environmental division and which Connor privately suspected was mostly a way to look scientific while gardening indoors.

His want was simple and slightly embarrassing: he wanted one judge, a single adult with a clipboard, to stand at his table long enough for him to show them the thing he had built. It was a pair of copper plates on a stand, a voltmeter, a ruler, and a worksheet he had designed himself, because Mr. Kaur, his physics teacher, had said at the start of the term that the fair needed "something you actually compute, not a volcano." Connor had taken this personally.

When a judge finally did stop, she was the youngest of them, maybe twenty-five, with a lanyard that said DR. SOMETHING obscured by her hair. She picked up his worksheet, read the top line, and frowned. "You've written that the field here is fifty volts per metre."

"That's what the plates give," Connor said, with the calm of a boy who had checked the arithmetic four times.

She looked at him for a moment, then at his ruler, then at the paper again, and then, in a gesture he would think about later with something close to vertigo, she handed the worksheet back and said, "Tell me how you got it," and walked away toward the coffee table by the bleachers. Just walked away. Behind him he heard Jade, who had abandoned her own table on fractals to come spectate, whisper, "She destroyed you."

Connor stood there recalculating in his head. Voltage divided by distance; he had written one hundred divided by two, because the gap was two centimetres, and two went into one hundred fifty times, and fifty had sat on his poster all morning in confident marker. He looked at the ruler. He looked at the poster. Somewhere in his chest an old certainty began to calcify into its true form, which was not certainty at all but habit.

Then, with a strange exhilaration, the kind that arrives only when something breaks in the right direction, he got out a fresh sheet. The distance between the plates was 0.02 metres. One hundred volts across a gap of 0.02 metres. He did the division slowly, as if the numbers might change if he rushed them, and they did not: five thousand. Volts per metre. His answer had been a hundred times too small, which was, he noted on the sheet in small letters, what forgetting to convert centimetres to metres cost you. He had known the conversion rule since he was eleven. Knowing it and using it turned out to be different activities.

Mr. Kaur appeared at the table while Connor was correcting the poster with a strip of paper and double-sided tape, having found the tape in Calista's bag of horticultural supplies. "Interesting fix," Mr. Kaur said, in the tone of a man who had seen this exact tape-based repentance before.

"Two centimetres is 0.02 metres," Connor said, pressing the paper flat over the old number. "I divided by two instead of 0.02. So the field between the plates is five thousand volts per metre, not fifty. Same plates, same hundred volts."

Mr. Kaur nodded once. "The judge came back while you were at my table getting tape, by the way. I told her you'd be a minute."

"She came back?"

"She's talking to the cress."

Calista looked up from her grow light with the expression of someone whose diurnal rhythms had been disturbed. "If she asks, the plants rotate toward the light every morning on a twenty-four-hour cycle, and I have data."

"She's not going to ask the cress anything," Jade said. "She's going to ask Connor why his poster looks like a ransom note."

The judge did come back, and she did ask, and Connor walked her through it: the copper plates, the gap of 0.02 metres, the hundred volts from the supply, the field of five thousand volts per metre between them, and then, because he did not want to pretend the morning had gone differently, the fifty. "I got it wrong first," he said. "I divided by centimetres. It was a hundred times too small." He had prepared a small speech about how errors in units propagate, but he abandoned it, because her face had the particular stillness of someone who had heard a lot of small speeches today.

She wrote something on her clipboard. "Most students patch over it," she said. "Yours is taped."

"It's double-sided tape," Calista offered from the next table. "Mine."

The judge almost smiled, moved on to the cress, and Connor stood by his plates listening to Calista explain germination to someone with a doctorate, his corrected poster catching the gymnasium light at a slight angle, the strip of paper already curling at one corner.

"Bring more tape next year," Jade said.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In the UK, a driver who passes the test in an automatic car may drive only automatic cars, and must pass a manual test to drive a manual car.
story:
Nathan's father had backed the family's manual car out of the driveway before leaving for work, which Nathan chose to interpret as a vote of confidence rather than an accident of parking. The driving school's car arrived at nine, silver and unnervingly clean, and the instructor, Mr. Traoré, got out holding a clipboard like a man serving papers.

"You booked automatic," Mr. Traoré said, looking at the clipboard, then at the manual car cooling in the street, then at Nathan, in a way that suggested he had done this arithmetic before.

"I booked the easier one," Nathan said. "I thought I'd build up to it."

"Build up to what?"

Nathan had prepared an answer on the walk from the front door to the driveway, roughly eleven seconds of thinking. "My dad's car. It's the only one I'd actually drive. Uni's forty minutes away and he works from home now, so it just sits there."

Raquel, who had come to watch because her Saturday contained nothing else, was sitting on the low garden wall with a mug of tea she had helped herself to from Nathan's kitchen. "Tell him about the loophole," she said. "He's got a loophole."

"It's not a loophole. It's a system." Nathan explained that you could pass in an automatic, get on the road sooner, and do the manual test later, at leisure, like a second language taken in the evening. Mr. Traoré listened with the patience of a man who had heard this particular sermon delivered from many pulpits.

"In the UK," Mr. Traoré said, "if you pass your test in an automatic, you can only drive automatics. You'd have to pass another test, a manual one, before you could touch your dad's car." He said it without emphasis, the way you report the weather, and let the silence do the rest.

Nathan felt the elegant system collapse into its components. The automatic lessons were cheaper to learn in, faster to pass, and, it now appeared, profligate in a hidden way, spending months of his life on a licence that would leave the family car untouchable, a museum piece he could admire through the window. Raquel was watching him with open enjoyment. "You look like a man who's just met maths," she said.

"It's not maths. It's casuistry. I was deciding which rules were real by figuring out which ones I wanted." He had done it before, he realized, with revision schedules and with Marie, whom he had told he was too busy to see, a position that had survived exactly until she stopped asking. Mr. Traoré unlocked the car.

"We can still start today," the instructor said. "Or I can move you to the manual car and you spend your first lesson stalling in this driveway while your friend drinks all your tea."

"That's the second cup," Raquel confirmed, holding up the mug.

Nathan looked at the manual car in the street, then at the automatic at the kerb, two silver vehicles separated by one hedge and a licensing distinction he had not known existed at breakfast. The honest position was that he did not know whether he was someone who took the quick door and paid later, or someone who paid now out of principle, and the driveway was not going to tell him. But the manual was the car he would actually drive, and a licence that enfranchised him in the family's one vehicle was worth more than a clean first lesson.

"Manual," he said. "I'll stall."

"Everyone stalls," Mr. Traoré said, and crossed to the driver's side to move the seat back, because Nathan was taller than the last seventeen people who had learned there.

Nathan settled behind the wheel. The clutch went down farther than he expected, like a pedal with somewhere else to be, and his first attempt at finding the biting point produced a shudder that travelled up through the handbrake and out the windows. The car lurched three feet and died. Raquel raised her mug from the wall.

"That counts as driving," she called. "I saw it move."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Japan's Buddhist festival of Obon, families light fires to welcome the spirits of ancestors home, and at the end many float lanterns down rivers to guide the spirits back.
story:
The machines had been turned off an hour before, and the room had gone quiet in a way Justin had not expected, as if silence were something the equipment had been producing all along. His grandfather lay under the sheet with his hands folded, and their grandmother stood at the window with her back to everyone, watching the parking garage change color in the late sun. Justin's mother was speaking to a nurse in the hallway, her voice low and even, the deposition of facts that hospitals require: time of death, who was present, what should be signed. Justin stayed by the bed because it seemed like someone should, and because if he moved he would have to decide where to go.

Tom found him there twenty minutes later, still in his work polo from the pharmacy, smelling faintly of hand sanitizer. He stood in the doorway for a while, which Justin appreciated, because Tom understood that some rooms are circumscribed by their grief and it isn't for other people to push the walls outward. Then he came in anyway and put a hand on Justin's shoulder and said, "Dude. I got you a vending machine coffee. It's terrible. It cost a dollar seventy-five and it's worth nothing."

"It's worth a dollar seventy-five," Justin said, and took it, and that was the first almost-laugh either of them had, standing over a dead man with bad coffee. Their grandfather would have liked it. He had been a man of terrible coffee himself, and of opinions about it, delivered with the confidence of someone who had never once brewed a good cup.

Jaidyn arrived next, out of breath from the stairwell because she refused elevators on principle, a principle she could not explain and had never tried to. She had known the grandfather less well, but she knew Justin, and she looked at him the way you look at someone to find out what shape they are in. "Your mom said I could come up," she said. "She's filling out forms forever down there. I think they gave her a whole notebook."

"That's the deposition," Justin said. "There's always more paper than you think."

The three of them ended up in the family lounge down the hall, under fluorescent lights that hummed at a pitch designed, Justin had always suspected, to keep anyone from getting too comfortable. There was a fish tank with one fish in it, and Jaidyn fed it a flake from the canister beside the tank even though a sign said not to. "He looks destitute," she said. "One fish in a whole tank, in a hospital. That's the saddest thing I've seen all day, and I just came from your grandfather's room, so."

"That's actually true," Justin said, and it was strange how the laugh came out of him, sideways and unwilling, but real.

It was Jaidyn who asked what would happen next, whether there would be a service, and Justin told them about the summer he was eleven, when his mother had shipped him to his grandmother's town outside Nagoya because she said he needed to know that side of the family and he suspected she needed a summer without him. He had been furious about it for the first two weeks, circumscribed by his own sulking, and then the festival had come and his fury had quietly dissolved without his permission.

"Obon," he said. "That's what it's called. In August. First the families light fires, little ones outside the house, and that's to welcome the spirits of the ancestors home. They come back for those days. That's the whole point. You light the fire and they find their way."

"Like a porch light," Tom said.

"Like a porch light for dead people, yeah. My grandfather built the fire that year in this little metal bowl, and he was so serious about it, and my grandmother put out the good dishes like company was coming. And then, at the end, after the visiting's over, everyone goes to the river and floats lanterns. You set them on the water and the current carries them down, and that's how the spirits find their way back. The lanterns go down the river and the spirits go with them."

"Back where?" Jaidyn asked.

"Back," Justin said. "I never asked. I was eleven. I thought it was a thing that happened to lanterns."

Ms. Castillo, the night nurse who had looked after the grandfather for the last three weeks, came into the lounge to say she was sorry, and to tell them the room would stay open as long as the family needed, no rush, and then she noticed the fish. "You fed him again," she said to Jaidyn, without heat. "He's on a diet. He's the only fish in this hospital and everybody loves him to death." She turned out the lounge lights on her way out, said the hallway ones would stay on, and Justin thought that was the whole job really, knowing which lights to leave on.

Afterward, in the parking garage, the three of them leaned on the concrete wall and looked at the city, at the river running through it, visible as a dark seam between the lit buildings. "So would your family do that here," Jaidyn said. "The lantern thing. Could you?"

"I don't know if you're allowed to just put things in the river," Tom said. "There's probably a form."

"There's always a form," Justin said. "We're at a hospital. Forms are the house style."

But he was already working it out, or letting it work itself out in him: that the fire and the lantern were both directions, one saying come home and one saying go safely, and that he had spent three weeks in a hospital learning the same two sentences without knowing it. He didn't know what he believed about spirits, and he wasn't going to pretend he did, and it occurred to him that this was fine, that the ritual didn't require his certainty, only his hands.

"August is five months off," Jaidyn said. "If we do it right. If we wait."

"Or," Tom said, "we build a fire tonight in your grandmother's little metal bowl, if she kept it, and in August we find a river and a lantern and we let the current do its part."

Justin looked at the water moving through the dark, unhurried, going where it had always been going. "She kept it," he said. "It's in the garage with the good dishes."

"Then get the matches," Jaidyn said. "I'll drive."

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: The STAR method structures an interview answer as Situation, Task, Action and Result, so a story about past experience ends with what actually happened.
story:
The invitation had said six o'clock, and Jason arrived at six-fifteen with his interview shoes on, because the interview was at eight and his mother had the car after that. Gabriel's backyard was already loud. String lights hung between the fence and the garage, and over the folding table where the cake would go, someone had stretched a diaphanous white sheet that caught the light and moved when the wind did, so the whole table looked like it was breathing.

"You're wearing a tie," Emrik said from the lawn chairs. "To a birthday party."

"It's for after," Jason said. "I have the Greene's interview at eight."

"The grocery store."

"The grocery store." Jason sat down on the arm of the chair. He had the printed page from the library folded into his back pocket, and he could feel its corner against him when he leaned, a small hard fact of the evening.

Gabriel came over with a paper plate of chips. "My brother interviewed there. He said the manager asks about your experience and you have to tell her a story, like a real one, with an ending. He rambled, he said. Talked four minutes about his paper route and never said what came of it. Didn't get the job."

"That's the thing," Jason said. "I don't know how to answer that question. When I practice I just start talking and then I'm somewhere else and I don't know how I got there."

Emrik pulled his phone out of his pocket, thumbed through it, held it out. "My cousin sent me this when she was job hunting. Look."

The screen showed a worksheet. Jason read it under the string lights, tipping the phone so Gabriel could see. Situation, Task, Action, Result. A way of building an answer so that a story about something you'd actually done arrived at what had actually happened. There was a line at the bottom of the worksheet, an example about restocking shelves, that ended with a number: the shift went faster and nothing ran out. Jason read it twice.

"So you start with where you were," he said slowly. "Then what you were responsible for. Then what you did. Then the result. The actual result. Not a feeling about it. What happened."

"You're teaching him this now," Gabriel said. "At my party."

"It's twenty to seven," Emrik said. "He has time. And you got a phone speaker and three friends. That's an interview panel."

They set it up behind the garage, away from the music. Gabriel sat on an overturned bucket with the phone held like a clipboard and said, in a low and startlingly good imitation of a tired manager, "Tell me about a time you handled a problem under pressure."

Jason opened his mouth and began, and within a minute he was describing the geometry class, then the fire drill during the geometry class, then a hallway, then something about Emrik's older sister's wedding, and Gabriel dropped the manager voice and said, "Stop. What was the question."

"I don't know," Jason said. "I prevaricate. When I don't know the ending, I just keep adding middle."

"Fine. Use the thing. Situation."

Jason put his hands flat on his knees. "Situation. Last summer, the community centre, the day camp. Task. I was the one who took attendance at the pool. Action. There was a kid missing from the count, and instead of standing at the fence yelling, I checked the change rooms first, then told the lifeguard, and we did the deck sweep in order. Result. He was in the change room, he'd gone back for his goggles, and we found him in under three minutes. Nobody panicked. The director changed the attendance sheet so goggles checks happened before the count." He stopped. His heart was going, but the answer had ended. It had actually ended, on something true.

"Again," Gabriel said. "Different question."

They ran it four more times. Once Jason lost the thread and Emrik just said, "Result," like a stage direction, and Jason picked it back up. Once Gabriel asked why he thought the deck sweep had worked, and Jason started to say something about luck, then stopped. "I can't prove the order mattered. It worked, that's all I can say happened." He looked at the sheet billowing over the cake table. "I don't want to pretend I know the causality of everything. I just did it and it turned out."

"That's honest," Emrik said. "The sheet doesn't say you have to explain why it worked. Just that it did."

Ms. Sandhu, who lived next door and had come over with a bowl of pasta salad, had been standing at the corner of the garage for some of this. "Practicing interviews in the dark," she said. "That's the most sensible thing happening at this party." She set the bowl on the upturned bucket. "Look at the top of his head, not the phone, when you listen. And when you answer, look up."

At ten to eight the cake came out, and the singing happened, and Jason ate half a slice standing up, and then his mother honked once from the street. He took the tie out of his back pocket, where the worksheet had been, because he had left the worksheet with Emrik, who was holding it up and mouthing Result at him over the candles.

The manager at Greene's had a small office behind the deli counter and a form on a clipboard. She asked about school, then she asked the question, the one about a time he handled something under pressure. Jason looked up from his own hands and began at the pool, and he watched her pen start moving when he reached the part about the change rooms, and it kept moving, all the way to the attendance sheet, all the way to the end of what had actually happened. She looked up when he finished, and the pen stopped.

"How old is this kid," she said, "the goggles kid."

"Eight," Jason said. "He was fine. He was proud of the goggles."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In a parliamentary system, the head of government, usually a prime minister, holds office by keeping the confidence of the legislature rather than by winning a separate popular election.
story:
The line outside the church hall moved in small shuffles, and Nathan kept his voter card folded into quarters in his fist, the way Kristina had told him to, though she had also told him it didn't matter. She was two places ahead with her mother, and Brodie was somewhere behind, late as always, having texted a photo of his own reflection in a bus window with the caption "voting for the first time, looking like an acolyte who wandered into the wrong ceremony." Nathan had laughed on the sidewalk and then stopped laughing when he realized he wasn't sure he could explain what he was about to do.

He had spent Sunday at his grandfather's apartment, the one with the balcony over the laundromat, and his grandfather had asked him the question over sandwiches. "Who are you voting for Thursday?" And Nathan had said the prime minister's name, because that was how everyone talked, and his grandfather had set down his sandwich and said, "Nobody voted for him." Nathan had argued. He had said people absolutely had, he'd seen the rallies on television. His grandfather, who had arrived from a presidential country decades ago and still thought in its grammar, said, "I voted for a president, once. A man. One name on one ballot. Here you show me a ballot with a local stranger on it and tell me it's for the man on television."

Nathan hadn't had an answer. He'd changed the subject to the leak in the grandfather's kitchen and gone home and looked things up until one in the morning, and what he found had rearranged something in him, not the way a fact settles into place but the way a door reveals that the room is larger than you thought. In the morning he texted Kristina, who was studying politics in her first year, and she wrote back a single line: "Confidence, not a separate election. Look it up properly, don't get it from memes." He looked it up properly. It was strange to him that a man could be the head of government, could be on the news every night, could shape so much, and hold it all by keeping the confidence of the legislature rather than by winning a vote with his own name on it. Strange, and then, after a while, not strange at all. It was like finding out the captain of a ship is chosen by the crew and can be replaced by the crew, which felt capricious and also felt like something the crew ought to be able to do.

Inside the hall, the folding tables were arranged with an officious neatness, and Ms. Clarke, who had taught him history in grade eleven and now, apparently, spent election days directing traffic, recognized him before he'd finished saying his name. "Nathan. You're old enough now. That's a strange thing for me." She pointed him to the correct table, and while the clerk turned pages in the binder, Ms. Clarke asked, "You know how it works, the counting, all that?" and he surprised himself by saying, "I didn't until this week. My grandfather asked me why nobody voted for the prime minister directly and I couldn't answer him." She nodded without explaining anything, which was her way, and said, "You'll vote for someone whose name you've never seen on a national stage, and the party that wins the most seats forms the government. That's a real thing to hold in your head on your way to the booth." Then the clerk handed him a ballot and a pencil with no eraser, and that seemed to presage something, though he couldn't have said what.

The booth was cardboard, shoulder-width, private in the flimsiest possible way. His grandfather's face was on the ballot with him, not literally, but the argument was, the sandwich set down on the plate, the old man's certainty that a vote should be for a man and not a mechanism. Nathan stood there a long moment with the pencil. He thought about how Brodie had voted early at the campus station and confessed afterward, in the coffee line, that he had simply picked the party his father hated, which struck Nathan as voting out of spite and therefore as worse than voting out of ignorance, though he hadn't said so. He thought about Kristina's line about confidence. In a parliamentary system, the prime minister keeps office by keeping the confidence of the legislature, not by winning a separate popular election, and every ballot Nathan had ever considered was a small piece of that arrangement, a vote for a local candidate that would become a seat, seats that would become a government, a government that could fall if it lost the room's support. Whether that was better than his grandfather's one-name ballot, whether it was more democratic or less, he genuinely did not know, and he tried to let not-knowing be part of the decision instead of a distraction from it.

He marked the ballot beside a name he had needed to look up that week, a woman who had taught adult literacy classes and whose flyer had come through the mail slot only once. He folded it twice the way the sign instructed and fed it into the box, and the machine made a soft mechanical swallow, and it was done, four years of eligibility culminating in ten seconds.

Outside, Brodie was arriving at a jog, shirt untucked. "Did I miss it? Tell me I didn't miss democracy."

"You didn't miss anything. The box is still hungry," Nathan said.

Kristina came out behind them, sealing her voter card back into her wallet. "My mom's still inside arguing with Ms. Clarke about whether the pencil counts as biased." She looked at Nathan. "So? Did you figure out your grandfather's thing?"

"I figured out the fact of it. Whether it's better, no."

"Good," she said. "That's the honest answer." She pulled her jacket tighter against the wind coming off the avenue, and nodded toward the church doors where her mother was still visible through the glass, gesturing with the pencil.

Brodie said, "Explain it to me while I'm in line. I want to sound smart at dinner tonight." Nathan followed him back toward the door, already sorting in his head which parts he could say out loud and which parts would have to stay folded, like the ballot, like quarters, until someone asked him directly.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Josef Albers made over 1,000 works in his Homage to the Square series from 1950 until 1976, keeping nested squares constant while changing only the colours.
story:
Nicholas spread the ten sheets across the kitchen table, weighting the curling corners with mugs and a jar of pencils, and tried to see them the way a stranger would. They were drawings of the same bridge over the creek behind his house, done at ten different hours, and he had been certain a week ago that this was his theme. Now the sheets looked like ten separate arguments that happened to share a subject, and the portfolio deadline sat nine days out with an artist's statement he could not start because he could not finish the sentence "My work is about."

Tatum arrived at four with a bag of clementines and no invitation, which was how she preferred it. She sat down across from him, peeled a clementine in one long ribbon, and began looking at the drawings without asking permission. "These are good," she said, in the tone she used when she meant the opposite of whatever comfort she was offering. "But you're hiding behind the bridge. Every single one is the bridge being interesting, not you being interesting." Tatum wanted the summer scholarship at the studio on Delancey more than she admitted to anyone, and she had decided that helping Nicholas was also a way of practicing for it, sharpening her eye on someone else's problem before she had to turn it on her own.

"That's a brutal thing to say about nine days of work," Nicholas said, but he didn't argue, because she was doing the thing he couldn't, reading the drawings from outside. He had been so busy rendering the rivets and the shadow of the railing that he'd never asked what the drawings were for. He pulled his laptop over and typed "series" into the search bar, half wanting a precedent, half wanting to be told it was fine.

He found Albers instead. Homage to the Square, a series of paintings he'd scrolled past in some textbook once and never slowed down for. Josef Albers made over 1,000 works in that series from 1950 until 1976, keeping the nested squares constant while changing only the colours. He read the sentence twice, then a third time, and something in his chest went quiet, the way it did in physics class when an equation suddenly described a thing he'd been watching happen for years. Over a thousand. Twenty-six years of the same four squares, the same proportions, and the only variable was colour. He turned the laptop so Tatum could see.

"One composition," she said, tilting her head. "That's either discipline or a weird way to sublimate an obsession." She was smiling, but her eyes had gone serious, the incipient plan visible in them before she said it aloud. "You should do that. Keep the bridge exactly the same, every drawing identical in structure, and change one thing."

"Light changes ten ways in nine days," Nicholas said, and even as he said it he understood how small that sounded. He gathered up the drawings, squared them, and dealt them out again in a fresh order, not by hour but by colour, dawn to dusk, and the table suddenly had a pulse to it, a sequence that moved. "The whole thing becomes one artwork with ten parts," he said slowly. "The theme isn't the bridge. The theme is what colour does to a fixed thing."

Ms. Demir, his old art teacher, had told him once that a portfolio was an argument, and he'd thought she meant it should be persuasive. Now he thought she might mean something closer to hermeneutics, that the ten pieces were a way of reading one object over and over, and that the statement was just the record of what he'd found in the reading. He got a clean sheet and wrote across the top: same bridge, different light. Then he crossed out "different light" and wrote "different colour," because light was an excuse and colour was the actual decision he'd been making without knowing it.

"Here's the problem," he said to Tatum, tapping the sheet of dawn drawings. "I only have three finished ones that keep the composition truly constant. I moved the viewpoint in the others. I'd have to redo them." Nine days. Redoing meant not polishing, meant submitting rougher work in service of a structure he believed in. He tried to hold both thoughts at once: that the constraint was the idea, and that the constraint might be too expensive now.

"Then redo them," Tatum said, already reaching for his good pencils. "I'll draw with you. I need the hours anyway." She pulled a blank sheet toward her side of the table and began blocking out her own version of the creek, low and wide, and Nicholas watched her for a second, then sharpened a pencil and pinned a fresh sheet where the first dawn drawing had been.

Outside, the light on the bridge was going amber at the edges of the day. He drew the first line of the railing and kept his hand steady on the second.
